planSummary.one_line: Four War-Carts leave the capital before turn 25 and take the nearest capital before it has Walls. Everything after turn 80 is a wide Science empire built on the cities they took and the Ziggurats laid behind them.

name: Gilgamesh
conditionCost: None
note: War-Carts expire as units but captured cities do not. Cleanest spike on the roster.

dates.historicity: legendary; possibly a historical king of Uruk, later deified

titles: Hero of the Epic of Gilgamesh

personality.temperament: The epic opens with a king too strong for his city, who wears out its young men and takes its brides, until the gods make him an equal, Enkidu, out of clay. The two fight, embrace, and go to kill the guardian of the cedar forest together. When Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh wanders the earth in a lion skin looking for a way not to. He comes home without one and looks at his walls.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Ally of Enkidu, seeks long alliances and defends his friends; the epic's whole second half is grief for one.

history.bio: Gilgamesh appears in the Sumerian King List as the fifth king of the first dynasty of Uruk, reigning 126 years, and in inscriptions of later kings who claimed him as a brother or a god. If he lived, it was around 2700 BCE, in the city on the Euphrates whose walls he is credited with building, nine kilometres of baked brick around what was then the largest settlement in the world. The poems about him were written in Sumerian by 2100 BCE and gathered into the Akkadian Epic of Gilgamesh by the end of the second millennium; the standard version, twelve tablets, was found in the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh in 1853. It tells of his friendship with Enkidu, the killing of Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, Enkidu's death, the journey to Utnapishtim who survived the flood, and the return to Uruk with nothing but the knowledge that the walls would outlast him. The walls are still there, a mound in the desert called Warka.
history.legacy: He is the first hero whose name is written down, and his story is the oldest one still read.

This rewards Gilgamesh for piling onto wars his allies have already started rather than starting his own.

civInfo.historical_background: Gilgamesh was the legendary king of the Sumerian city-state of Uruk, likely based on a real ruler from around 2700 BCE, and is the hero of the Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest surviving works of literature. The epic recounts his friendship with the wild man Enkidu, their shared adventures and battles against monsters, and Gilgamesh's grief-driven quest for immortality after Enkidu's death. That central friendship is directly reflected in his Civ VI leader ability, Adventures of Enkidu, which rewards fighting alongside allies rather than alone. Uruk itself was one of the world's first true cities, and Gilgamesh was famed for building its great walls.

name: Amanitore
conditionCost: Nubian Pyramids want desert-adjacent placement
note: Dual-banks: conquest AND permanently cheaper districts. Survives its own spike better than most.

personality.temperament: The record of Amanitore is in stone, not in words. Her name stands beside Natakamani's on temples at Naqa, Amun's great hall at Meroë and the restored sanctuary at Jebel Barkal. The Lion Temple shows her striding, broad-shouldered, a sword raised over bound captives. The kandakes of Kush ruled as warriors and builders, and she was shown as both. Rome's writers noted queens in Meroë and did not name her.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, City Planner, favours leaders who build districts; the historical Amanitore's reign is the most productive building period in Meroitic history.

history.bio: Amanitore ruled the Kingdom of Kush from Meroë, on the Nile between the fifth and sixth cataracts, in the first half of the first century CE. She held the title kandake, queen, and governed alongside Natakamani, who may have been her husband or her son; the inscriptions name them together and give her equal size and equal regalia. Their reign was the last great age of Meroitic building. They restored the temple of Amun at Meroë, built the Lion Temple and the Amun temple at Naqa, repaired Jebel Barkal and raised reservoirs along the river. Kush had treated with Augustus a generation earlier and now traded with Rome in gold, ivory and iron. Her pyramid stands at Meroë in the northern cemetery, steeper and smaller than Egypt's, and robbed long before archaeologists reached it. The Meroitic script on her monuments has still not been read in full.
history.legacy: She built more of Kush than any ruler before or after her, and her name is on all of it.

civInfo.historical_background: Amanitore was a Kandake (ruling queen) of the Kingdom of Kush, centered at Meroë in what is now Sudan, reigning in the 1st century CE alongside her co-ruler Natakamani. Nubian kandakes held real political and sometimes military authority, a tradition distinct from many neighboring cultures, and several are remembered leading armies in defense of their kingdom. Amanitore and Natakamani presided over an extensive building program, constructing and restoring temples and pyramids at Meroë, Naqa, and elsewhere, which is echoed in-game by the civilization's pyramid improvement and its strong bias toward dense urban district construction.

name: Montezuma
conditionCost: Combat strength scales with luxury variety, so needs wide territory
note: Captured Builders are permanent infrastructure. Luxury bonus decays in relevance as strength numbers inflate.

dates.historicity: historical; Civ VI's Montezuma draws on both Moctezuma I and II

titles: Ilhuicamina (He Who Shoots Arrows at the Sky)

personality.temperament: The game's Montezuma, with his feathers and his hunger for luxuries, is a composite, but the conqueror who built the empire was the first of the name. Moctezuma Ilhuicamina took the Triple Alliance beyond the Valley of Mexico, codified its laws, decreed the sumptuary rules that told each rank what it could wear, and after famine instituted the flower wars that fed the temples with captives. He raised the Great Temple and built the aqueduct from Chapultepec. The captives are part of the record, not a footnote.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Tribute, wants the luxuries his neighbours have and resents those who hold them; the Aztec state ran on tribute lists.

history.bio: Moctezuma Ilhuicamina was born around 1398, the son of the tlatoani Huitzilihuitl, and was elected ruler of Tenochtitlan in 1440 after serving his half-brother Itzcoatl as general and chief adviser. With Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco he pushed the Triple Alliance south across the mountains into Morelos and east to the Gulf coast, bringing Chalco, Cuauhnahuac and the Huastec cities under tribute. The great famine of 1450 to 1454 nearly broke the city; afterwards he and his adviser Tlacaelel formalised the xochiyaoyotl, the flower wars with Tlaxcala and Huexotzinco fought to take prisoners for sacrifice. He rebuilt the Templo Mayor, built the dike of Nezahualcoyotl across the lake against floods, laid the aqueduct from Chapultepec, founded the botanical garden at Huaxtepec and issued the sumptuary laws that ordered Aztec society by dress. He died in 1469. His great-grandson Moctezuma II, who received Cortés, carried the name to its end.
history.legacy: He made Tenochtitlan an empire and gave it the laws, the temple and the wars that defined it until the Spanish came.

civInfo.historical_background: Montezuma (Moctezuma II) was the ninth tlatoani (emperor) of the Aztec Empire, ruling from 1502 until 1520 at the height of its territorial power, commanding a tribute-based empire across central Mexico. He is best known historically for his fateful encounter with Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés in 1519, which set in motion the fall of Tenochtitlan and the Aztec Empire within two years. Aztec economic and religious life depended heavily on luxury goods and tribute, which is reflected in his in-game ability tying luxury resources directly to happiness and combat strength.

name: Tomyris
conditionCost: None
note: Highest-risk spike. Duplicate units and heal-on-kill produce zero standing yield. Pure tempo.

history.polity: Massagetae, a Scythian people east of the Caspian

personality.temperament: Herodotus says Cyrus asked for her hand and she understood he was asking for her kingdom. She offered him a fair fight on either side of the river. He took her son by a trick, a feast with wine left for the Massagetae to find; the son killed himself in captivity. She sent Cyrus a message that she would give him his fill of blood, beat his army, and put his head in a skin of it. Herodotus had heard several versions and chose that one as the most credible.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Backstab Averse, likes leaders who keep their word and hates those who betray friends; Cyrus broke a parley to take her son.

history.bio: Tomyris was queen of the Massagetae, a nomadic people of the steppe east of the Caspian Sea and beyond the Araxes, around 530 BCE. Herodotus, writing a century later, says that Cyrus the Great, having taken Babylon, sought to marry her and was refused, bridged the river to invade, and on Croesus's advice left a camp stocked with wine as a trap. The Massagetae under her son Spargapises took the camp, drank, and were captured; Spargapises killed himself. Tomyris then met Cyrus in the hardest battle, Herodotus says, that barbarians ever fought, and the Persians were destroyed and Cyrus killed. She filled a skin with human blood and put his head in it. Other ancient writers give Cyrus other deaths, and no Persian record describes his end. The Massagetae left kurgans, horse burials and gold across the steppe, but no writing, and Tomyris survives only in the history of her enemies' enemies.
history.legacy: She is the queen who, in the only account that survives, killed the greatest king of her age for the death of her son.

terrain.why: Horses and Kurgans on flat land
Open ground for Saka Horse Archers

affinity.barbarianStance: Scythian units heal on kills and strike wounded enemies harder. Every camp is a free promotion and free healing; clear all of them with the two-for-one horsemen.

rivals.why: Tomyris killed Cyrus in the record; the game remembers

civInfo.name: Tomyris

leader_ability.name: Killer of Cyrus
leader_ability.text: All of Tomyris's units gain a large Combat Strength bonus when attacking wounded (damaged) enemy units, and heal a significant amount of health whenever they eliminate a unit, rewarding aggressive follow-up strikes on weakened targets.

agenda.name: Backstab Averse
agenda.text: Tomyris favors leaders willing to become her Declared Friends, but strongly dislikes anyone who launches Surprise Wars, especially against a former friend or ally.

civ_ability.name: People of the Steppe
civ_ability.text: Training any light cavalry unit, or the unique Saka Horse Archer, produces two units for the price of one, giving Scythia an unmatched early-cavalry rush capability.

unique_units.name: Saka Horse Archer
unique_units.notes: A ranged cavalry unit that, combined with the civ ability, is produced in pairs, giving Scythia overwhelming early mounted numbers.

unique_infrastructure.name: Kurgan
unique_infrastructure.notes: A unique tile improvement built on flat land that generates Faith and Gold, giving Scythia useful yields even as a mobile, cavalry-focused civilization.

civInfo.historical_background: Tomyris was queen of the Massagetae, a confederation of Iranian-Scythian nomadic peoples on the Central Asian steppe, in the 6th century BCE. She is remembered chiefly for defeating and killing Cyrus the Great of Persia in battle around 530 BCE after he invaded her territory, reportedly having his corpse's head placed in a wineskin filled with blood in retribution for her son's death at his hands. That victory over Cyrus is the direct namesake of her leader ability, Killer of Cyrus, and her agenda's suspicion of surprise wars mirrors the treachery she associated with the Persian invasion.

history.polity: Gran Colombia (Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama); Peru; Bolivia

personality.temperament: He was a rich orphan who swore on a hill in Rome to free his country and spent the fortune doing it. He crossed the Andes in winter with an army in rags, lost and won and lost again, and freed six countries. He wrote the constitution of Bolivia with a president for life and watched the republics he made turn on each other and on him. He said that he who serves a revolution ploughs the sea. He died of tuberculosis on the way to exile, forty-seven, with his boots and shirt borrowed.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Campaña Admirable, likes leaders who keep their units close to home and dislikes those who send armies near his borders; his wars were liberations and he read any other army as an invasion.

history.bio: Simón Bolívar was born in Caracas in 1783 to one of the richest families in Venezuela, orphaned by nine, and educated by the republican tutor Simón Rodríguez and in Europe. He joined the junta that deposed the Spanish governor in 1810 and, after the first republic fell, led the Admirable Campaign of 1813 that retook Caracas. He was driven out again in 1814, wrote the Jamaica Letter from exile, returned with Haitian help in 1816, and in 1819 crossed the flooded llanos and the Andes to beat the Spanish at Boyacá and take Bogotá. He proclaimed Gran Colombia and won Venezuela at Carabobo in 1821; Sucre won Ecuador at Pichincha in 1822; Bolívar won Peru at Junín in 1824 and Sucre finished it at Ayacucho. Upper Peru became Bolivia in his name in 1825. The union then came apart: Venezuela seceded, an assassination attempt in 1828 nearly killed him, and in 1830 he resigned and set out for Europe. He died at Santa Marta on 17 December 1830.
history.legacy: He freed six nations from Spain and lived to see them refuse the union he had built for them.

quote.text: He who serves a revolution ploughs the sea.
quote.source: Letter to General Juan José Flores, 9 November 1830

civInfo.historical_background: Simón Bolívar was the preeminent leader of the early 19th-century Spanish American wars of independence, liberating what are now Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Peru, and Bolivia from Spanish colonial rule. Revered across Latin America as 'El Libertador,' he envisioned a unified South American state, Gran Colombia, which he helped found in 1819 but which fractured into separate nations shortly after his death in 1830. His campaigns depended on rapid, long-distance cavalry movement across difficult terrain, reflected in-game by his civilization's extra-movement and rapid-promotion abilities and the mobile Llanero cavalry unit named for the horsemen of the Venezuelan plains who formed the backbone of his armies.

expansionOrigin: Persia and Macedon Civilization & Scenario Pack

history.polity: Kingdom of Macedon and the empire it conquered

personality.temperament: Alexander could not stay still. He slept little, drank hard, wept at the deaths of friends and killed one of them in a quarrel. He led from the front and carried the wounds to prove it. Plutarch records a man who wanted glory more than land and who asked his tutor, Aristotle, for more worlds. His soldiers followed him past the edge of every map they knew.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Short Life of Glory, rewards leaders at war and scorns those at peace; the historical Alexander fought for eleven of his thirteen years as king.

history.bio: Alexander came to the throne of Macedon at twenty, in 336 BCE, after his father Philip was murdered at a wedding. Within two years he had burned Thebes and crossed into Asia with forty thousand men. At the Granicus, at Issus and at Gaugamela he broke the armies of Darius III, and by 331 the Persian Empire was his. He took Egypt and was named pharaoh, founded Alexandria, burned Persepolis, and marched east through Bactria into the Punjab, where his army refused to go further. He turned back along the desert coast and died in Babylon in June 323 BCE, aged thirty-two, of a fever or a poison; the sources disagree. He left no settled heir. His generals divided the world he had taken, and the Greek language, Greek cities and Greek gods settled in it for three centuries after him. Cities fell to him by the hundred; the people in them were sold or spared at his mood.
history.legacy: He conquered the known world in eleven years and left it to be fought over for forty.

quote.text: There is nothing impossible to him who will try.
quote.source: Attributed to Alexander; recorded in later collections, not in a contemporary source

civInfo.historical_background: Alexander the Great became king of Macedon in 336 BCE and, within thirteen years, conquered the entire Persian Empire, extending Macedonian rule from Greece to Egypt and northwest India before his death at age 32 in 323 BCE. His conquests spread Greek (Hellenistic) language, art, and institutions across the ancient world, blending with local cultures in the regions he took — the direct inspiration for Macedon's civ ability, which lets the empire absorb bonuses from captured cities rather than simply destroying them. After his death his generals, the Diadochi, carved his empire into rival successor kingdoms, and his relentless campaigning without ever losing a battle is echoed by his agenda's restless preference for a civilization always at war.

name: Gorgo
conditionCost: Requires a continuous supply of things to kill
note: Culture banks into unlocked civics permanently, which is why she outlasts other combat-trigger leaders.

dates.display: Queen consort of Sparta c. 490 to 480 BCE
dates.historicity: historical; known through Herodotus and Plutarch

personality.temperament: Herodotus tells of her at eight or nine warning her father not to be bribed by a Milesian with a case for war; the king sent the man away. When a blank wax tablet came to Sparta she was the one who guessed the message was under the wax. Asked by an Athenian woman why Spartan women alone ruled their men, Plutarch has her say, because we alone give birth to men. She sent Leonidas to Thermopylae with instructions to marry a good man and bear good children.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, With Your Shield or On It, respects leaders who never give up cities and despises those who do; her husband's three hundred did not retreat.

history.bio: Gorgo was the only child of Cleomenes I, king of Sparta of the Agiad line, and was born around 518 BCE. She married her uncle Leonidas, who succeeded to the throne in about 490 after Cleomenes died, mad or murdered, in prison. Herodotus, who wrote within living memory, gives her two of the few recorded sayings of any Spartan woman and credits her with reading the secret message from Demaratus that warned Greece of Xerxes' invasion. In 480 Leonidas marched north with three hundred Spartans and died at Thermopylae holding the pass; their son Pleistarchus was a child, and Gorgo's brother-in-law Cleombrotus and then her nephew Pausanias held the regency. Her later life is unrecorded. Sparta kept no histories of its own, and what survives of Gorgo is what Athenians and a Boeotian chose to remember: a girl who was listened to, and a queen who told the truth in one sentence.
history.legacy: She is the one Spartan woman whose words the Greeks wrote down, and they were all about not yielding.

quote.text: Because we are the only women who give birth to men.
quote.source: Plutarch, Sayings of Spartan Women, Gorgo 5

civInfo.historical_background: Gorgo was queen of Sparta and wife of King Leonidas I, one of the few women of the ancient Greek world whose political wisdom and outspokenness were specifically recorded by the historian Herodotus. Leonidas famously led 300 Spartans (with allied Greek forces) in a last stand against the invading Persian army at the Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BCE, an event directly named in Gorgo's leader ability. Spartan culture prized unyielding martial resolve, epitomized by the (possibly apocryphal) saying attributed to Spartan mothers urging sons to return from battle 'with your shield, or on it' — the namesake of Gorgo's agenda, which rewards refusing to back down in war or negotiation.

name: Ambiorix
expansionOrigin: New Frontier Pass: Byzantium & Gaul Pack
conditionCost: Bonus only holds while units stay clustered
note: Positioning discipline is the cost. Falls apart in wide-front late-game wars.

history.polity: Eburones, a Belgic tribe of Gaul

personality.temperament: Everything known of Ambiorix comes from the man who hunted him. Caesar presents him as a talker who could turn a Roman officer's trust into a trap, and a fighter who knew when to leave a field. He parleyed, lied, ambushed, and vanished into the forest with four horsemen when the legions came for him. The Eburones were destroyed for his sake; he was never caught.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Scourge of Rome, dislikes leaders who build large armies; the historical Ambiorix was the Belgic king who nearly broke Caesar's hold on Gaul.

history.bio: Ambiorix ruled half the Eburones, a Belgic people between the Meuse and the Rhine, under Caesar's occupation of Gaul. In the winter of 54 BCE, with a Roman legion and five cohorts quartered on his land, he persuaded their commanders, Sabinus and Cotta, that a general rising was coming and that he would see them safely to another camp. He ambushed the column in a valley and destroyed it, the heaviest Roman loss of the whole war. He then raised the Nervii and Aduatuci and besieged Quintus Cicero's camp until Caesar himself broke the siege. In 53 BCE Caesar invited every tribe in Gaul to plunder the Eburones and marched through their country with fire. Ambiorix escaped across the Rhine with a few riders, and the record ends there. Nineteenth-century Belgium made him a national hero and put his statue in Tongeren, the Roman town that replaced his people.
history.legacy: He destroyed a legion by talking to it, and the Romans erased his nation to find him.

civInfo.historical_background: Ambiorix was chieftain of the Eburones, a Belgic tribe in northeastern Gaul (modern Belgium), who led a major uprising against Julius Caesar's occupying Roman legions in 54 BCE, annihilating an entire Roman legion and inflicting one of Rome's worst defeats during the Gallic Wars. Caesar's brutal reprisal campaign nearly exterminated the Eburones, though Ambiorix himself reportedly escaped and vanished from history. He is remembered today, especially in Belgium, as an early symbol of resistance to Roman conquest, directly reflected in his in-game agenda 'Scourge of Rome' and his ability rewarding militarization and unit concentration reminiscent of guerrilla-style Gallic warfare.

planSummary.one_line: Fence the empire with Ikandas and walls, bank eight Impi, and do nothing offensive until Mercenaries. Then pair every Impi into a Corps the same turn, take the nearest capital, and let each capture upgrade the unit that took it.

name: Shaka
conditionCost: Genuinely weak until Mercenaries
note: Auto-upgrade on capture is a compounding loop, not a flat bonus. Strongest ramp in the category.

personality.temperament: He was an illegitimate son driven out with his mother, and he came back with a short stabbing spear and a new way of fighting. He drilled his regiments barefoot over thorns, forbade them to marry, and ordered the enemy's wounded killed and his own cowards executed on the field. He built a kingdom of a quarter of a million in a decade. When his mother died he ordered the nation to mourn for a year without crops or milk, and had thousands killed for not weeping enough. His half-brothers stabbed him.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Paramount Chief, likes leaders who form corps and armies and dislikes those with scattered units; the impi fought as a single body.

history.bio: Shaka was born around 1787 to Senzangakhona, chief of the small Zulu clan, and Nandi, a Langeni woman, in a union his father's people did not recognise. Mother and son were driven out and he grew up among the Mthethwa, where he became a soldier of Dingiswayo. He took the Zulu chieftaincy about 1816 with Dingiswayo's backing and replaced the throwing spear with the iklwa, a short stabbing blade, replaced sandals with bare feet for speed, and organised his men into age regiments with the bull-horn formation of a centre and two enveloping wings. By 1824 he ruled from the Pongola to the Tugela and his wars had set the whole interior in motion, the mfecane, which emptied and remade southern Africa. He received the first British traders at Port Natal and sent envoys to the Cape. His mother Nandi died in 1827 and his grief became terror. On 22 September 1828 his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana murdered him at his kraal. Dingane took the kingdom.
history.legacy: He made a clan of a few thousand into a nation and an army, and the shock of it reorganised half a continent.

His reforms fueled the Zulu Kingdom's rapid expansion and contributed to the wider upheaval and displacement across the region known as the Mfecane. His emphasis on organized, disciplined regiments is mirrored in-game by his leader ability's early access to Corps and Armies.

planSummary.one_line: Stage four Immortals, two Archers and a Battering Ram on the target's border, declare the Surprise War on turn 46, and take the capital inside the ten turns of +2 Movement. A second ten-turn burst before turn 90 takes a second city or a second neighbour; after that the grievances are the ceiling and Persia is a domestic trade and Pairidaeza Culture civilization.

name: Cyrus
expansionOrigin: Persia and Macedon Civilization & Scenario Pack
conditionCost: Surprise War diplomatic and grievance penalties
note: Ten-turn window, repeatable but never banked. The trap case for the whole Spike tier.

titles: King of the Four Corners of the World

personality.temperament: The Greeks, who had every reason to hate Persia, admired him. Xenophon made him the model of a just king and Herodotus gave him a childhood out of legend. The clay cylinder he left in Babylon speaks of restoring temples and sending exiles home, and the Hebrew prophets called him anointed. He moved faster than his enemies expected and treated the conquered as subjects rather than spoil.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Opportunist, likes leaders who declare surprise wars and dislikes those who never do; Cyrus took Lydia by marching in winter when Croesus had sent his army home.

history.bio: Cyrus became king of the Persians at Anshan around 559 BCE, a vassal of the Medes, and within a decade had overthrown his overlord Astyages and taken Ecbatana. In 547 or 546 he marched on Lydia, fought Croesus to a draw at Pteria, and then followed him home to Sardis in the off-season and took the city. The Greek cities of Ionia fell to his generals. In 539 he entered Babylon, the sources say without a battle, after the Euphrates was diverted or the garrison opened the gates. He let the Jews return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple, kept the Babylonian gods in their shrines and himself in the local titles, and governed through satraps and roads. He died in 530 BCE campaigning in Central Asia against the Massagetae; Herodotus says Queen Tomyris had his head put in a skin of blood. His tomb at Pasargadae is a plain stone house on six steps, and Alexander, who found it looted, had it restored.
history.legacy: He built the largest empire the world had seen and governed it by leaving its peoples their gods.

He was noted for relatively tolerant governance of conquered peoples, exemplified by the Cyrus Cylinder, and for a career built on swift, decisive military campaigns — reflected in his ability's rewards for surprise warfare. Cyrus was ultimately killed in 530 BCE in battle against Tomyris and the Massagetae, a fitting rival matchup within Civilization VI given her leader ability is literally named for his death.

conditionCost: Requires trade route setup before each target

personality.temperament: Temüjin was abandoned by his clan as a boy, enslaved, and hunted; he killed his half-brother over a fish. As khan he rewarded loyalty above birth, promoted a herdsman to general and a captured enemy archer to the head of his army, and made treachery to any master, even his enemy, a capital crime. He asked Taoist sages about immortality and let every faith pray for him. He emptied cities that resisted.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Horse Lord, likes leaders with strong cavalry and resents those who field it against him; the Mongol army was horse, bow and nothing else.

history.bio: Temüjin was born on the Onon river around 1162 to a minor chieftain who was poisoned when the boy was nine. He spent his youth hunted, captured and freed, and built a following from the dispossessed. By 1206 he had defeated or absorbed every tribe on the steppe and was proclaimed Chinggis Khan at a great assembly. He reorganised the Mongols into decimal units with no regard to clan, issued a written law, and turned outward. He broke the Western Xia, took Beijing from the Jin in 1215, and when the Khwarazmian shah murdered his envoys in 1219 he destroyed that empire in three years; Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv and Nishapur were depopulated. His generals rode around the Caspian and beat the Russian princes on the Kalka. He died in August 1227 on campaign against Xia, from a fall or a wound, and was buried in secret. His sons and grandsons ruled from Korea to Hungary.
history.legacy: He took a scattered people and made them the largest land empire in history, and the cities that refused him were erased.

His campaigns were also marked by devastating psychological warfare and rapid conquest, a legacy echoed in-game by a leader ability that lets Mongol cavalry armies grow stronger by absorbing defeated enemy horsemen.

planSummary.one_line: Settle toward the nearest neighbour, bank four Varu and a Ram-and-Swordsman team before Military Training, then declare a War of Territorial Expansion and take two cities in the ten turns the +5 and +2 Movement last. Repeat on the next neighbour while Varu still outclass the field; after turn 100 India is a Stepwell and Dharma civ that holds what it took.

name: Chandragupta
conditionCost: Only fires on Wars of Territorial Expansion, so needs an adjacent target
note: Doubly gated: right war type AND inside the timer.

personality.temperament: Greek sources knew him as Sandrokottos, a young man who had seen Alexander's camp and judged that an empire could be taken. Indian tradition gives him a teacher, Chanakya, whose treatise on statecraft counsels spies, bribes and surprise. He took the throne by force, held it with a vast army and a vaster bureaucracy, and at the end, the Jain accounts say, gave it up and starved himself to death as a monk.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Boundless Ambition, pushes him to expand into any neighbour's land; the historical Chandragupta took the whole of northern India in twenty years.

history.bio: Chandragupta rose from obscure origins in the Magadha country in the years after Alexander's withdrawal from the Indus. Around 321 BCE, guided by the Brahmin strategist Chanakya, he overthrew the Nanda dynasty and took Pataliputra on the Ganges. He then pushed west into the Punjab, drove out the Macedonian garrisons, and in 305 met Seleucus I, Alexander's successor in Asia, in war. The peace that followed gave Chandragupta the provinces of the Hindu Kush and gave Seleucus five hundred war elephants and a marriage alliance. Seleucus's envoy Megasthenes lived at his court and wrote of a city nine miles long, an army of six hundred thousand, and a king who feared assassination enough to sleep in a different room each night. His empire ran from Afghanistan to Bengal. Late in life he abdicated for his son Bindusara, followed the Jain teacher Bhadrabahu south to Shravanabelagola, and died there by ritual fast.
history.legacy: He founded the first empire to hold most of India and gave it up to die as a monk.

civInfo.historical_background: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire around 321 BCE, unifying most of the Indian subcontinent for the first time in history with guidance from his strategist advisor Chanakya, traditionally credited as author of the Arthashastra — the classical treatise on statecraft and military strategy directly named in Chandragupta's leader ability. His empire laid the foundation later expanded and famously ruled with a turn toward Buddhist pacifism by his grandson, Ashoka. India's long history as home to numerous major religions living alongside one another is reflected in the civ ability Dharma, which rewards accommodating multiple faiths within the same cities rather than enforcing religious uniformity.

He fled to Kiev, then to Constantinople, where he led the emperor's Varangian axemen in Sicily, Bulgaria and the Holy Land, came home with a ship's hold of gold, and bought half a kingdom with it. He composed poetry, blinded a Byzantine emperor if the sagas are believed, and burned Hedeby. He died with an arrow in the throat, charging, at fifty-one.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Last Viking King, likes leaders with strong navies and dislikes those without; he crossed the North Sea with three hundred ships.

history.bio: Harald Sigurdsson was half-brother to Olaf II of Norway and fought beside him at Stiklestad in 1030, where Olaf was killed and Harald, wounded at fifteen, escaped east. He served Yaroslav of Kiev and then, from about 1034, the Byzantine emperors as a commander of the Varangian Guard, campaigning in Sicily and the Balkans and amassing a fortune. He returned north in 1045, married Yaroslav's daughter, and forced his nephew Magnus to share the Norwegian crown; Magnus died a year later and Harald ruled alone. He fought Denmark for fifteen years without taking it, founded Oslo, and crushed the old chieftains at home, earning the name Hardrada. In 1066, invited by Tostig Godwinson, he invaded England to claim its throne. He won at Fulford and five days later, on 25 September, was killed at Stamford Bridge by Harold Godwinson's army. Three weeks after that Harold fell at Hastings. The Viking age is usually dated to end with Harald.
history.legacy: He fought from Kiev to Sicily to York, and his death at Stamford Bridge is where historians end the Viking age.

terrain.why: Longships heal in neutral water and coastal raiding pays
Stave Church faith from woods and production for ships
Norway starts cold; Dance of the Aurora fixes it

affinity.barbarianStance: Coastal camps spawn galleys that pillage Norway's boats. The first Longship clears them and raids back; inland camps are cleared only if they can see a city.

civInfo.name: Harald Hardrada

leader_ability.name: Thunderbolt of the North
leader_ability.text: Grants a large Production bonus toward naval melee units and enables coastal raiding (pillaging coastal tiles and cities directly from naval melee units), and unlocks the unique Viking Longship, supporting an aggressive naval-raiding playstyle. (Harald also has an alternate 'Varangian' persona, added later, with a different ability, Varangian Guard, focused on cheaply levying and maintaining city-state units.)

agenda.name: Last Viking King
agenda.text: Harald wants to build a powerful navy, respects other civilizations with strong naval forces, and looks down on those with weak ones.

civ_ability.name: Knarr
civ_ability.text: Norwegian units can cross Ocean tiles once Shipbuilding is researched, suffer no extra Movement cost for embarking or disembarking, and naval melee units can heal even in neutral (unowned) territory, giving Norway unmatched early naval mobility.

unique_units.name: Berserker
unique_units.notes: A strong early melee unit that gains a further boost once Military Tactics is researched, fitting Norway's aggressive coastal-raiding identity.

unique_units.name: Viking Longship
unique_units.notes: A cheaper, faster, and stronger early naval unit than the Galley it replaces, able to heal in neutral waters thanks to the Knarr civ ability, ideal for early raiding.

unique_infrastructure.name: Stave Church
unique_infrastructure.notes: Provides Faith and additional benefits, and in the Varangian persona also grants Influence points, supporting Norway's religious and diplomatic play alongside its raiding.

civInfo.historical_background: Harald Hardrada ('Hard Ruler') was King of Norway from 1046 to 1066 and is often called the last great king of the Viking Age. Before taking the Norwegian throne he spent years as a mercenary commander in the Byzantine Empire's elite Varangian Guard, the historical basis for his alternate in-game persona. He died in 1066 at the Battle of Stamford Bridge in England while attempting to conquer the English throne, a defeat just weeks before the Norman Conquest that many historians treat as marking the symbolic end of the Viking Age — a fittingly aggressive, sea-borne legacy reflected in Norway's naval-raiding leader ability and civ-wide ocean mobility.

planSummary.one_line: Build Gold and Envoys across the river while city-states build the soldiers, then rent their armies at Castles with Black Army riding inside them and take cities you keep. If no neighbour is in reach, the same Envoys are a Diplomatic game.

name: Matthias Corvinus
conditionCost: Ongoing gold and envoy spend; levied units are rented, not owned
note: Captured cities are permanent but the army itself never is. Cash flow is the whole constraint.

history.polity: Kingdom of Hungary (and Croatia, Bohemia in part, Austria)

personality.temperament: He was elected king at fourteen by nobles on the frozen Danube, having spent the previous year as a prisoner in Prague, and he spent the next thirty-two years making sure no noble could do to him what they had done to his brother. He built the first standing army in Europe since Rome, the Black Army, and paid for it by taxing everyone. He collected the second largest library in Christendom, married an Italian, and took Vienna. Hungarian folklore made him the just king who walked among the poor in disguise.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Raven King, likes leaders who levy city-state troops and dislikes those who hold the city-states he wants; the Black Army was mostly mercenary.

history.bio: Mátyás Hunyadi was the younger son of János Hunyadi, the general who had held the Turks at Belgrade, and was elected king of Hungary in January 1458 after his elder brother had been executed by the previous king. He was fifteen. He broke the magnates who had elected him, reformed the courts and the tax system, and from about 1462 built the Black Army, a permanent force of some twenty to thirty thousand paid soldiers, largely Bohemian and German mercenaries, with artillery and a Danube flotilla. He fought the Ottomans at Jajce and Šabac but chose not to pursue a war of reconquest; he fought instead to the west, took Moravia and Silesia from Bohemia, and in 1485 captured Vienna and most of Lower Austria from the Emperor Frederick III. His court at Buda and Visegrád was the first Renaissance court north of the Alps, and his Bibliotheca Corviniana held some two thousand codices. He died in Vienna in April 1490, leaving a bastard son the nobles refused; the army was disbanded, and Hungary lost Mohács within forty years.
history.legacy: He raised Europe's first standing army since Rome and the greatest library north of Italy, and both were gone within a generation of his death.

terrain.why: Thermal Baths and river districts across from the city centre
Hungary's bias; Fire Goddess and the Thermal Bath

cityStates.why: Levied units get +2 Movement and +5 Strength
Buildings for the levied army's cities

affinity.barbarianStance: Hungary's army is borrowed from city-states. Protect the nearest city-state from camps, levy its units when a camp threatens, and keep your own production for buildings.

civInfo.name: Matthias Corvinus

leader_ability.name: Raven King
leader_ability.text: Units levied from city-states gain bonus Movement and Combat Strength, cost far less Gold and resources to upgrade, and levying troops from a city-state grants 2 extra Envoys there, making city-state levying a core Hungarian military strategy.

agenda.name: Raven Banner
agenda.text: Matthias Corvinus frequently levies units from city-states and admires other leaders who do the same, while disliking those who avoid using mercenaries.

civ_ability.name: Pearl of the Danube
civ_ability.text: Districts and buildings built across a River from the City Center receive a large Production bonus, rewarding cities founded and developed along rivers.

unique_units.name: Black Army
unique_units.notes: An early professional-army unit that upgrades directly into Hungary's second unique unit, giving Hungary a long-lasting line of powerful cavalry-adjacent forces.

unique_units.name: Huszár
unique_units.notes: A strong light cavalry unit that continues Hungary's unique military line into the medieval era, well suited to levied-army compositions.

unique_infrastructure.name: Thermal Bath
unique_infrastructure.notes: Provides Amenities and helps prevent revolt/loyalty problems in newly conquered or levy-heavy cities, supporting Hungary's mercenary-driven playstyle.

civInfo.historical_background: Matthias Corvinus ruled the Kingdom of Hungary from 1458 to 1490, nicknamed 'the Raven King' for his family's raven emblem (Corvinus), and is remembered as one of Renaissance Europe's most capable rulers. He built the Black Army of Hungary, one of Europe's first large professional standing armies, financed partly through mercenaries and levied forces, directly reflected in his in-game ability and agenda around cheaply levying city-state units. He also turned his court at Buda into a major center of Renaissance humanism, attracting scholars and artists from across Europe, and his Hungary sat astride the Danube, echoed by the civilization's river-adjacency production bonus.

planSummary.one_line: Play a plain wide builder for 110 turns, reach Gunpowder with Niter, an Armory and Ibrahim already promoted in the forward city, then take capitals with Janissaries behind Bombards that hit walls harder than anyone else's.

name: Suleiman
leaderTitle: Suleiman I, The Magnificent (also known as Kanuni, "The Lawgiver")
conditionCost: Nothing early, which is also the problem
note: No meaningful Ancient-era identity. Needs a survival plan for the first 100 turns.

personality.temperament: Europe called him the Magnificent and his own people called him the Lawgiver, and he was both: he besieged Vienna and he wrote the code that ran the empire for three centuries. He wrote poetry under the name Muhibbi, the lover, much of it to Hürrem, the slave he freed and married against every custom. He had his friend Ibrahim strangled, his son Mustafa strangled in front of him, and died in his tent at the siege of Szigetvár, which was kept from the army until the fortress fell.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Lawgiver, likes leaders with large standing militaries and dislikes those who do not match him; the Janissaries were the first modern standing army in Europe.

history.bio: Suleiman succeeded his father Selim I in September 1520, at twenty-five, as sultan of an empire that already held Syria and Egypt. He took Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes from the Knights in 1522, destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács in 1526 and killed its king, and in 1529 besieged Vienna and failed in the autumn rain. He took Baghdad from the Safavids in 1534 and most of Hungary in 1541, and his admiral Barbarossa made the Mediterranean an Ottoman sea. He rewrote the kanun, the secular law of the empire, settled the taxes and the land system, built the Süleymaniye with Sinan and rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. He married Hürrem, a Ruthenian slave, and had his eldest son Mustafa executed in 1553 on suspicion of treason. He died on 6 September 1566, in the night, in his tent before Szigetvár, at seventy-one. The empire never again had a reign like his.
history.legacy: He ruled the Ottoman Empire for forty-six years at its height, besieged Vienna, and wrote the laws that outlived his line.

terrain.why: Production for the Grand Bazaar's siege army
Growth for conquered cities that keep their amenities

affinity.barbarianStance: Ottoman siege units are for walls, not camps. Clear the nearest two with warriors and build the Barbary Corsairs to keep the coast clean.

civInfo.name: Suleiman
civInfo.leader_title: Suleiman I, The Magnificent (also known as Kanuni, "The Lawgiver")

leader_ability.name: Grand Vizier
leader_ability.text: Suleiman gains access to a unique, exclusive Governor (Ibrahim) with strong military and diplomatic bonuses, and unlocks the Janissary unique unit plus a bonus Governor Title once Gunpowder is researched. It lets the Ottomans field an elite late-game army while also running a top-tier governor for loyalty and diplomacy.

agenda.name: Lawgiver
agenda.text: Suleiman keeps his own cities happy and loyal, and is impressed by civilizations that do the same or have founded many cities; he dislikes leaders whose cities are unhappy, disloyal, or few in number due to conquest.

civ_ability.name: Great Turkish Bombard
civ_ability.text: Ottoman siege units are trained 50% faster and gain +5 Combat Strength when attacking or defending against district defenses, making the Ottomans exceptionally strong at both offensive sieges and city-state coercion.

unique_units.name: Janissary
unique_units.notes: Cheaper and stronger than the Musketman, starts with a free promotion, and can convert a defeated enemy unit into an Ottoman unit, letting Ottoman armies grow while attacking.

unique_infrastructure.name: Grand Bazaar
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Bank in the Commercial Hub, is the cheapest unique building in the game, and adds bonus Amenities and access to extra strategic resources.

civInfo.historical_background: Suleiman I (r. 1520-1566) presided over the Ottoman Empire at its territorial and cultural zenith, pushing its borders deep into Hungary and the Middle East while his fleets contested the Mediterranean. Ottomans called him 'Kanuni' (the Lawgiver) for his sweeping legal and administrative reforms that brought consistency to a sprawling multiethnic empire, while Europeans knew him as 'the Magnificent' for his court's wealth and patronage of architecture (including the Süleymaniye Mosque) and the arts. His reign relied heavily on the elite, gunpowder-armed Janissary corps and an efficient siege-focused military, both reflected in the Ottomans' in-game strengths. This mix of centralizing governance and relentless military expansion is the throughline connecting the historical sultan to his in-game kit of governance-boosting abilities and siege-crushing bombards.

template.principle: The hardest template to write and the most necessary. The leader contributes nothing for 80 to 120 turns. Without an explicit early game AND an explicit statement that the flatness is intended, players abandon the plan around turn 60.

structure.goal: Survive, develop, and quietly accumulate the prerequisite the payoff phase consumes.
structure.opening_statement: State plainly at the top: Suleiman has no leader advantage during this phase. That is expected. The kit pays later and pays large. Do not evaluate this leader before turn 110.
steps: Run a complete generic build order. The guide must supply this in full, because the leader supplies no direction.
Maintain a defensive floor. Elimination during Phase A is the single most common way these leaders lose, and it is invisible in the ability description.
Accumulate the prerequisite even though it produces nothing yet: Siege-capable production base and the unique governor already placed in position
Provide non-ability progress markers so the player has feedback: city count, science rate, district count. Something must be visibly improving.

structure.goal: The kit switches on. Verify the accumulated prerequisite is actually sufficient.
steps: Check the stockpile. Activation with an empty stockpile wastes the entire dormant phase.
Peak. Siege specialization against fortified capitals.
Reorient production toward the payoff. Phase A build habits are now wrong.

structure.goal: Convert the accumulated position at speed. The remaining game is short, so this phase runs hot.
steps: Still functional.
Push the victory condition directly. There is no time for a second build-out.

abort_branch.trigger: Reaching activation with the prerequisite stockpile empty, or having lost cities during the dormant phase.
actions: Accept a lesser victory path built on the generic empire rather than the leader ability.
The leader ability is now decorative. Say so and stop planning around it.

template.fail_state: Crippled or eliminated before activation, or arriving at activation with nothing stockpiled. Both are Phase A failures that only become visible in Phase B.
anti_patterns: A thin early game. This is where the player spends most of their turns and all of their patience.
Omitting the flatness statement. Players read a flat curve as a mistake and switch strategies at exactly the wrong time.
Framing Phase A as preparation only. It also has to be survivable on its own terms.

planSummary.one_line: Govern every city for Toqui's Culture and experience, carpet the mountain Appeal with Chemamull, and keep a cavalry force ready so that whenever a neighbour enters a Golden Age you ride in, kill inside their borders, and let the Loyalty do the conquering.

name: Lautaro
conditionCost: Depends entirely on other civs entering Golden Ages
note: Only leader whose trigger is owned by someone else. Reactive by design.

personality.temperament: He was taken as a boy to be a Spanish officer's groom and spent three years watching horses, muskets and the way the invaders fought. Then he went home and taught his people to fight back in relays, to lure cavalry into ground that horses could not cross, and to ride the horses they captured. He killed the governor who had owned him. He was twenty-three when a surprise attack at dawn ended him, and the war he started lasted three hundred years.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Spirit of Tucapel, likes leaders who keep their cities loyal and dislikes those who lose them; he fought the Spanish for the land itself.

history.bio: Lautaro, Leftraru in Mapudungun, was captured around 1546 at the age of about eleven and served Pedro de Valdivia, conqueror and governor of Chile, as a page and groom. He escaped in 1550 or 1551 with a knowledge of Spanish horsemanship, armour and tactics. The Mapuche elected him toqui in 1553. At Tucapel in December of that year he attacked Valdivia's column in waves, exhausting the Spanish horse, destroyed it, and killed Valdivia. At Marihueñu in 1554 he destroyed a second army and burned Concepción, and burned it again in 1555. In 1556 he marched north on Santiago itself, through plague and famine, and in April 1557, camped on the Mataquito river, was surprised at dawn by Francisco de Villagra's cavalry and killed with most of his men. His head was displayed in Santiago. The Arauco War he began did not end until the 1880s, and Chile named warships, streets and a lodge of independence after him.
history.legacy: He learned the invaders' war as their servant and turned it on them, and the Mapuche held their land for three centuries after.

terrain.why: Chemamull on high-appeal tiles beside mountains
Production and defence

pantheons.why: Faith from appeal, which the Chemamull also uses

cityStates.why: Kabul's experience for the loyalty war

affinity.barbarianStance: The Toqui's experience bonus is against civilizations in a Golden Age, not camps. Clear camps for safety with Malón Raiders and keep the loyalty war for the neighbour.

civInfo.name: Lautaro

leader_ability.name: Swift Hawk
leader_ability.text: Defeating an enemy unit in enemy territory reduces the Loyalty of that unit's origin city, and Lautaro's units get a combat bonus when fighting civilizations that are in a Golden or Heroic Age, letting him punish and destabilize thriving rivals through raiding.

agenda.name: Spirit of Tucapel
agenda.text: Lautaro works to keep Loyalty high in his own cities and dislikes other civilizations that let their own cities' Loyalty slip, favoring stable, well-governed rivals.

civ_ability.name: Toqui
civ_ability.text: Cities with an established Governor gain bonus Culture, Production, and combat experience for trained units, and radiate Loyalty pressure toward nearby Mapuche cities, letting the Mapuche use Governors to both develop and hold their territory against Loyalty pressure.

unique_units.name: Malón Raider
unique_units.notes: A hard-hitting raiding cavalry unit that gains a combat bonus near friendly territory and can pillage for a single movement point, ideal for hit-and-run war-of-attrition strategies that punish rival Loyalty.

unique_infrastructure.name: Chemamull
unique_infrastructure.notes: A high-Appeal-requirement tile improvement that converts Appeal into Culture (and Tourism after Flight), making it a strong late-game culture/tourism engine for high-Appeal Mapuche territory.

civInfo.historical_background: Lautaro was a young Mapuche man captured and pressed into service by Spanish conquistador Pedro de Valdivia in 16th-century Chile, during which time he learned Spanish cavalry and siege tactics from the inside. He escaped and used that knowledge to lead Mapuche forces in the Arauco War, most famously defeating and killing Valdivia at the Battle of Tucapel in 1553. His guerrilla-style raiding tactics and refusal to hold static ground helped the Mapuche resist full Spanish conquest for centuries, longer than almost any other indigenous American people, a legacy echoed in his in-game focus on mobile raiding and loyalty-destabilizing warfare against more 'settled' golden-age rivals.

planSummary.one_line: Settle eight to ten cities before turn 80 on free Monuments, free Trading Posts and free roads, choose by turn 60 whether the Legions take a neighbour or the cities take Campuses, and spend the Culture lead on the civics that serve that choice.

name: Trajan
conditionCost: None
note: Free Monument in every city is the definition of a compounding, unconditional bonus. Beginner-safe.

personality.temperament: The Senate voted him the title Optimus, the best, and for a thousand years prayed that each new emperor be luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan. He was the first emperor born outside Italy, a career soldier adopted by an old man who needed the army's loyalty. He marched with his men, founded a welfare fund for poor children, built a harbour, a forum, a market and a column, and took the empire to its largest extent. He was fond of wine and of boys and the historians note both without heat.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Optimus Princeps, likes leaders who expand and dislikes those with small empires; Rome under him reached its widest borders.

history.bio: Marcus Ulpius Traianus was born in 53 CE at Italica in Spain, the son of a consul, and commanded legions on the Rhine and the Danube. Nerva adopted him in 97 to secure the army and died in January 98; Trajan took the throne without entering Rome for a year. He fought two wars against Decebalus of Dacia, in 101 to 102 and 105 to 106, destroying the kingdom and taking its gold mines, and told the story in the spiral relief of his column. He annexed Nabataea in 106. He spent the Dacian treasure on the Forum of Trajan, Trajan's Market, the baths on the Esquiline, the harbour at Portus and roads and bridges across the provinces, and he set up the alimenta to feed poor children in Italy. In 113 he went east, took Armenia and in 116 marched down the Tigris to the Persian Gulf, the only Roman to see it. Revolts behind him forced a withdrawal; he died at Selinus in Cilicia in August 117. Hadrian, named heir on the deathbed, gave the east back.
history.legacy: He took Rome to its greatest size and built so well in the capital that the Senate called him the best of all princes.

terrain.why: Roads and Baths for a wide empire
Legion production

affinity.barbarianStance: Rome expands faster than it defends. Each new city gets a Legion escort; the Legion clears the camp that was there and builds the fort.

civInfo.name: Trajan

leader_ability.name: Trajan's Column
leader_ability.text: Every city Trajan founds or acquires gets an extra free building in its City Center slot beyond the normal one (a Monument if still in the Ancient Era, or the era-appropriate equivalent later), giving Rome a permanent head start on infrastructure in every city, new or old.

agenda.name: Optimus Princeps
agenda.text: Trajan tries to bring as much territory as possible under his empire's control and looks down on civilizations that hold only a small amount of territory.

civ_ability.name: All Roads Lead to Rome
civ_ability.text: All Roman cities start with a free Trading Post, roads are automatically built to new cities within trade range of the Capital, and Gold income from Trade Routes passing through Roman cities is increased, giving Rome an economic and connectivity edge from the earliest turns.

unique_units.name: Legion
unique_units.notes: A stronger, more expensive Classical-era melee unit that doesn't require Iron and carries a builder charge it can spend to construct a Roman Fort, build a road, or harvest a resource in the field.

unique_infrastructure.name: Bath
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Aqueduct (must be built adjacent to the City Center and a water/mountain feature) and provides Amenities alongside its Housing bonus, making Rome's early cities more comfortable to grow.

civInfo.historical_background: Trajan ruled the Roman Empire from 98 to 117 AD and pushed it to its greatest territorial extent, conquering Dacia (for its gold) and campaigning into Mesopotamia and Armenia against Parthia. He is remembered as one of the 'Five Good Emperors' for combining military conquest with an ambitious building program: Trajan's Forum, Trajan's Market, and Trajan's Column (commemorating the Dacian Wars) all still stand in Rome today. His reputation for expanding territory while simultaneously building up infrastructure at home directly informs his in-game kit, which rewards both extra city buildings and holding maximal territory.

planSummary.one_line: Settle cities three tiles apart along the coast, pin a four-district cluster in each before anything is built, and let half-price Theater Squares and Holy Sites plus full adjacency from every neighbouring district carry a Culture game that the Electronics Factory finishes.

name: Hojo Tokimune
conditionCost: Tight city spacing; rewards planning discipline
note: Terrain-agnostic, which is rare. Works on almost any start. Beginner-safe.

personality.temperament: He was eighteen when the Mongol envoys came, and he had them turned away; when they came again he had them beheaded. He studied Zen with Chinese masters, built Engaku-ji for the dead of both sides, and is said to have asked his teacher Mugaku Sogen how to face the invasion and been told to cut off the source of fear. He answered the Mongols with walls and with a refusal that did not change.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Bushido, likes leaders whose faith and culture match their military strength and dislikes those who field armies without them.

history.bio: Hōjō Tokimune was born in 1251, the son of the regent Tokiyori, and became shikken, regent for a child shogun and the real ruler of Japan, in 1268 at eighteen. That year Kublai Khan's envoys arrived demanding submission. Tokimune refused them. In November 1274 a Mongol-Korean fleet landed in Hakata Bay with perhaps thirty thousand men, fought a day against the samurai of Kyushu, and withdrew in a storm. Tokimune executed the next embassies, in 1275 and 1279, and built a stone wall twenty kilometres long around the bay. In the summer of 1281 two fleets, some four thousand ships and a hundred and forty thousand men by the chronicles, were held on the beaches for seven weeks and then destroyed by a typhoon, the kamikaze, the divine wind. Tokimune founded Engaku-ji in Kamakura to pray for the dead of both sides, and died in 1284 at thirty-three. The shogunate, unable to pay the samurai who had fought, outlived him by fifty years.
history.legacy: He refused the Mongols twice and the sea finished the argument; Japan was not invaded again for seven centuries.

terrain.why: Districts on coast get Meiji adjacency and Samurai defend the shore
Production for the Electronics Factory later

naturalWonders.why: Defensive bonus and food at sea

pantheons.why: Districts faster in every new city

affinity.barbarianStance: Divine Wind gives +5 strength on coast and shallow water; coastal camps die to Samurai. Clear every camp on the coast, walls on the inland cities.

rivals.why: Harald raids the coast Hojo defends

civInfo.name: Hojo Tokimune

leader_ability.name: Divine Wind
leader_ability.text: Japanese land units get +5 Combat Strength on land tiles adjacent to Coast, and naval units get +5 Combat Strength in shallow water; Encampment, Holy Site, and Theater Square districts are also built in half the normal time, making Japan strong at coastal warfare and fast at fielding military/cultural/religious infrastructure.

agenda.name: Bushido
agenda.text: Tokimune favors civilizations that pair a strong military with high Faith and Culture output, and disapproves of civilizations that are militarily powerful but weak in Faith and Culture.

civ_ability.name: Meiji Restoration
civ_ability.text: Japanese districts receive the full (standard) adjacency bonus from being placed next to other districts, instead of the reduced 'minor' bonus other civilizations get, letting Japan pack districts tightly together for outsized yields.

unique_units.name: Samurai
unique_units.notes: A stronger Medieval-era melee unit that suffers no combat penalty when damaged, letting it keep fighting effectively even at low health.

unique_infrastructure.name: Electronics Factory
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Factory; a late-game production building that keeps Japan's tightly-packed district cities industrially competitive.

civInfo.historical_background: Hojo Tokimune served as regent (shikken) of Japan's Kamakura shogunate from 1268 to 1284, a period defined by the Mongol Empire's two attempted invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281. Tokimune organized Japan's samurai defenses and coastal fortifications to repel both invasions, and the second fleet was famously destroyed by a typhoon the Japanese called 'kamikaze,' or 'divine wind' -- the direct namesake of his in-game leader ability. A devout patron of Zen Buddhism, he is remembered as a symbol of samurai resolve and Japan's successful defense of its coastline, which the ability's coastal combat bonuses and fast military infrastructure evoke directly.

planSummary.one_line: Every Builder after the second is wonder fuel: four charges at 15% each is most of an Ancient or Classical wonder, and six to eight of them stand in your cities by turn 110. After that the ability is spent and China is a Culture civilization living in the most permanent assets in the game.

name: Qin Shi Huang
conditionCost: Builder charges spent on wonders are charges not spent on improvements
note: Wonders are the most permanent asset in the game. Best conversion rate of any spike.

dates.display: King of Qin 247 to 221 BCE; First Emperor 221 to 210 BCE

history.polity: State of Qin; the Qin dynasty, first unified Chinese empire
history.faith: Chinese state religion; Legalism in governance; sought immortality through alchemy

personality.temperament: He took the title huangdi, august sovereign, because king was no longer large enough. He standardised the script, the axle width, the weights and the coinage, burned the books that disagreed with him and, the histories say, buried the scholars who wrote them. He survived three assassination attempts and stopped sleeping in the same palace twice. He sent expeditions for the elixir of life and drank mercury for it. He was buried under a mountain with an army of clay.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Wall of 10,000 Li, dislikes leaders who build more wonders than he does; his tomb complex employed seven hundred thousand labourers.

history.bio: Ying Zheng was born in 259 BCE at Handan, a hostage prince's son, and became king of Qin at thirteen in 247. He took the government at twenty-two, dismissed his regent Lü Buwei, and with the Legalist minister Li Si and the generals Wang Jian and Meng Tian destroyed the six rival kingdoms one by one between 230 and 221 BCE. He proclaimed himself Shi Huangdi, First Emperor, abolished the feudal states for thirty-six commanderies, unified the writing system, the currency, the measures and the width of cart axles, built roads and canals, and joined the northern walls into a single frontier against the Xiongnu. In 213 he had the histories and classics of the other states burned; in 212, by Sima Qian's account, he had four hundred and sixty scholars buried alive. He toured his empire five times seeking immortality from magicians and died on the fifth tour, in 210 BCE, probably of the mercury he took. His dynasty fell four years later. His tomb at Lintong, guarded by eight thousand terracotta soldiers, has not been opened.
history.legacy: He made one China out of seven kingdoms and one script out of many, and his dynasty outlived him by four years.

terrain.why: Production for wonders; the Great Wall on the border
Growth under the wonders

naturalWonders.why: Chinese wonder with Great General points

pantheons.why: Wonders faster on top of Builder charges

affinity.barbarianStance: Crouching Tigers behind the Great Wall make camps harmless. Clear the camp that sees the capital and then stop; the Builders are for wonders.

civInfo.name: Qin Shi Huang

leader_ability.name: The First Emperor
leader_ability.text: Builders can be spent to instantly complete 15% of the original cost of Ancient and Classical era Wonders, and Builders gain an extra build charge, letting Qin Shi Huang rush out early Wonders far faster than other civilizations.

agenda.name: Wall of 10,000 Li
agenda.text: Qin Shi Huang likes civilizations that don't compete with him for Wonders and that build Wonders themselves; he strongly dislikes losing a Wonder race to another civilization.

civ_ability.name: Dynastic Cycle
civ_ability.text: Earning a Eureka or Inspiration grants an extra flat percentage of Science or Culture toward the associated Technology or Civic, and completing a Wonder grants a free Eureka and Inspiration, reinforcing China's wonder- and tech-rushing playstyle.

unique_units.name: Crouching Tiger
unique_units.notes: A cheaper ranged siege unit with strong ranged strength but shorter range than the Field Cannon it replaces, giving China an efficient siege option.

unique_infrastructure.name: Great Wall
unique_infrastructure.notes: A unique defensive tile improvement that generates Gold (more when connected to adjacent wall segments) and grants a large defensive Combat Strength bonus to units standing on it.

civInfo.historical_background: Qin Shi Huang unified China's warring states in 221 BCE to become its first emperor, founding the short-lived but transformative Qin dynasty. He standardized China's writing system, currency, weights and measures, and road networks, and connected and extended existing regional walls into the precursor of the Great Wall of China -- the direct basis for China's in-game unique improvement. He is equally famous for the enormous Terracotta Army buried to guard his tomb, and for a harsh, centralizing rule that built lasting state infrastructure at great human cost. His fixation on grand unifying construction projects and standardization is mirrored in his in-game ability to rush Wonders and China's civilization-wide bonus for converting breakthroughs into further progress.

context.condition_cost: Builder charges spent on wonders are charges not spent on improvements
context.condition_check: the condition is met: Builder charges spent on wonders are charges not spent on improvements

era_role.medieval_renaissance: Ability expired. Living off the wonders already banked.
era_role.industrial_modern: Ordinary civ with an unusually good wonder collection.

caveats: Charges spent on Wonders are charges not spent on tile improvements, so the terrain stays weak.
A rival completing the wonder first wastes the charges entirely with no refund.

guide_requirements: A wonder shortlist with pre-planned fallbacks for each one being sniped.
A Builder charge budget explicitly split between wonders and improvements.
The era boundary where the ability stops, treated as a scheduled transition.

template.principle: The ability has an expiry. The guide is a timer wrapped around a conversion deadline. Its most important content is not the build order, it is the turn the plan stops and what replaces it.

structure.goal: Reach the window with everything already staged. Nothing in this phase is optional; staging done after the window opens is spent from the budget.
steps: Turn 1: identify the target. Qin Shi Huang's window is short enough that target selection cannot wait for scouting to finish.
Turns 1-15: scout toward the target only. Exploration away from the target is a luxury this shape cannot afford.
Turns 10-30: production goes to the units or charges the window will consume. Infrastructure that pays back after 110 is deferred.
Pre-window checkpoint: confirm the condition is met: Builder charges spent on wonders are charges not spent on improvements, and that units are within striking distance, not at home.

structure.goal: Convert tempo into permanent assets. Cities, wonders, or improvements. Not kills, not gold, not map presence.
core_loop: Each turn, ask: is the objective closer than it was last turn?
If the answer is no for three consecutive turns, the window is failing. Go to the abort branch.
Track remaining turns explicitly. The player should always know the number.

checkpoints.test: Is at least half the objective secured?
checkpoints.if_no: Reduce scope now. Take one city instead of three. Partial conversion beats total expiry.

checkpoints.test: Has the tempo become something permanent?

structure.goal: Stabilize what was taken. This phase is longer than both prior phases combined and most guides for this shape underwrite it badly.
steps: Amenity and loyalty audit on every acquired city before any new construction.
Infrastructure catch-up: the arming phase deliberately skipped this, and the bill comes due now.
Choose a victory path. From here the era leads and the kit follows. Ordinary civ with an unusually good wonder collection.

abort_branch.trigger: Window closed with no permanent gain, or three stalled turns before the midpoint.
actions: Make peace immediately. Prolonging a failed window converts a bad position into a lost game.
Disband surplus units. The maintenance is now pure loss.
Switch to the generic development plan for the empire you actually have.

template.fail_state: The window closed and nothing permanent was gained. Qin Shi Huang is now an ordinary civ with an army it cannot afford and grievances it cannot repay.
anti_patterns: Writing Phase 3 as an afterthought. It is most of the game.
Expressing the deadline as a turn number only. Tie it to opponent tech where possible, since that is what actually closes the window.
Letting the player believe a large army at 110 counts as success. It does not.

planSummary.one_line: Settle wide, give every city a Commercial Hub and a Hansa before it has the population to deserve them, decide by turn 60 whether the extra Military slot buys a city-state and a neighbour or just the escorts, and point the Production at Campuses and a Spaceport.

name: Frederick Barbarossa
conditionCost: Extra district needs population and production to actually fill
note: The district cap break compounds with every city founded. Scales with empire size, not era.

personality.temperament: Red-bearded, broad, courteous in speech and relentless in purpose, he spent his reign trying to make the empire a fact rather than a title. He crossed the Alps six times to make the cities of Lombardy obey and burned Milan when they would not. He treated with popes and made antipopes. He died at nearly seventy in a river in Anatolia, in armour, on his way to Jerusalem; the legend has him asleep under a mountain waiting to come back.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Iron Crown, dislikes leaders who ally with or hold city-states he wants; he spent thirty years fighting the free communes of Italy.

history.bio: Frederick of Hohenstaufen, duke of Swabia, was elected king of Germany in 1152 as a compromise between the Welf and Staufen factions that had torn the kingdom. Pope Adrian IV crowned him emperor in Rome in 1155. He issued the Roncaglia decrees in 1158 claiming the regalian rights of the Lombard cities, and the cities refused him; he razed Milan in 1162, lost his army to malaria outside Rome in 1167, and was beaten by the Lombard League at Legnano in 1176. He made peace at Constance in 1183, keeping the title and conceding the substance. In Germany he broke the power of Henry the Lion, settled the eastern marches, and married his son to the heiress of Sicily. In 1189 he took the Third Crusade east with the largest army of the three. On 10 June 1190 he drowned crossing the Saleph river in Cilicia, and his army dissolved.
history.legacy: He spent thirty-eight years making the Holy Roman Empire mean what its name said, and drowned on the way to Jerusalem.

Commercial Hubs and farms around the Hansa triangle

pantheons.why: Faster first districts in every city

rivals.why: Pericles protects the city-states Frederick conquers

civInfo.name: Frederick Barbarossa

leader_ability.name: Holy Roman Emperor
leader_ability.text: Frederick gets an additional Military policy card slot and +7 Combat Strength when his units attack city-states, making him a formidable coercer and conqueror of city-states specifically.

agenda.name: Iron Crown
agenda.text: Frederick prefers civilizations that stay out of city-state affairs, and dislikes leaders who become suzerains of city-states or who conquer them.

civ_ability.name: Free Imperial Cities
civ_ability.text: German cities can build one additional District beyond what their Population would normally allow, letting Germany build wider, more district-dense cities than any other civilization.

unique_units.name: U-Boat
unique_units.notes: A cheaper Modern-era submarine with a combat bonus in ocean tiles and extra sight, giving Germany an efficient naval raiding tool.

unique_infrastructure.name: Hansa
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Industrial Zone; it gains adjacency bonuses from any resource (not just mines/quarries) and extra Production next to a Commercial Hub, making it a powerful, flexibly-placed production district.

civInfo.historical_background: Frederick I 'Barbarossa' (red beard) ruled as Holy Roman Emperor from 1155 to 1190, spending much of his reign trying to reassert direct imperial authority over the fractious Italian city-states and princely territories that nominally owed him fealty -- a struggle his in-game agenda around city-states is built on. A leading figure of the Crusades, he drowned crossing a river in Anatolia while leading forces on the Third Crusade, and German legend later held that he was merely sleeping beneath a mountain, ready to return and restore Germany's greatness. That legacy of a fragmented Germany striving to hold its component territories together under central authority is echoed in the German civilization's extra-district ability, which lets Germany's cities exceed normal size limits the way the Holy Roman Empire itself sprawled beyond normal medieval state boundaries.
