planSummary.one_line: Settle in the mountains, feed each city with Terrace Farms and domestic Trade Routes, put a Campus against three mountain faces in every city, and let the tallest cities on the map carry a Science game that Machu Picchu and mountain Universities accelerate.

name: Pachacuti
conditionCost: Mountain terrain dependency; dead start without it
note: Turns the map's worst tiles into workable ones. Highest start-roll variance on the roster.

dates.historicity: historical; from Spanish-era chronicles of Inca oral history

personality.temperament: His name means he who overturns the world, and the chroniclers say he took it after the day the Chanka came for Cusco and his father and elder brother fled. He stayed, won, and remade everything: the city in the shape of a puma, the sun temple sheathed in gold, the roads, the storehouses, the census, the calendar, Machu Picchu as his estate. He moved whole peoples across the mountains to break resistance. He retired and let his son conquer.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Sapa Inca, likes leaders who stay off his continent and dislikes those who settle on it; Tawantinsuyu meant the four quarters of the world.

history.bio: Cusi Yupanqui was a younger son of the Inca Viracocha, ruler of the small Cusco kingdom in the Andes. When the Chanka confederation attacked Cusco around 1438 and his father withdrew, he led the defence, won, and took the throne and the name Pachacuti. In thirty years he turned Cusco into Tawantinsuyu, conquering the Titicaca basin, the central highlands and the coast, and sending his son Topa Inca north to Quito. He rebuilt Cusco in stone, raised the Coricancha to the sun, and ordered the terraces, storehouses, roads and way stations that let the state move armies and grain across four thousand kilometres of mountain. He resettled conquered peoples as mitimaes far from home, fixed the quipu records and the labour tax, and built the royal estate at Machu Picchu. He gave up the campaigns to his son around 1463 and died in Cusco in 1471. Sixty years later Pizarro's men found the empire he had made and took it in two years.
history.legacy: He turned a mountain town into the largest empire in the Americas and built the roads that are still there.

terrain.why: Terrace Farms, the Qhapaq Ñan, and citizens working mountain tiles
Terrace Farms on hills beside mountains

pantheons.why: Faith from quarries in the hills

affinity.barbarianStance: Mountains block raiders as well as settlers. Settle in the valleys, hold the passes with Warak'aq, and clear only the camps that share your valley.

civInfo.name: Pachacuti

leader_ability.name: Qhapaq Ñan
leader_ability.text: Domestic Trade Routes gain bonus Food for every Mountain tile near their origin city, and the Incas gain access to the Qhapaq Ñan unique tile improvement once the Foreign Trade civic is researched, rewarding mountain-heavy empires with strong internal trade.

agenda.name: Sapa Inca
agenda.text: Pachacuti wants to settle his own cities near Mountains and is happy to let other civilizations avoid that terrain, but dislikes rival leaders who also settle near Mountains and compete with him for that land.

civ_ability.name: Mit'a
civ_ability.text: Incan citizens can work Mountain tiles directly for Production (with an increased yield reached in the Industrial Era), and Mountains provide bonus Food to adjacent Terrace Farms, letting the Inca build thriving cities in terrain other civilizations must avoid.

unique_units.name: Warak'aq
unique_units.notes: A ranged unit with notably higher Ranged Strength than the Skirmisher it replaces, giving the Inca strong early ranged offense to complement their mountain-based defense.

unique_infrastructure.name: Terrace Farm

unique_infrastructure.name: Qhapaq Ñan

civInfo.historical_background: Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui ruled from roughly 1438 to 1471 and is credited with transforming the small kingdom of Cusco into the vast Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu) through a combination of military conquest and sweeping administrative reform. He is traditionally credited with commissioning Machu Picchu and with building out the empire's remarkable road network, the Qhapaq Ñan, which linked its Andean territories across extremely difficult mountain terrain -- the direct namesake of his in-game leader ability and unique improvement. His empire's mastery of mountain agriculture, especially terrace farming, let the Inca feed large populations in terrain most other pre-modern states avoided, which is exactly what his in-game civilization ability rewards.

name: John Curtin
conditionCost: Requires being attacked, which you do not control

titles: Leader of the Australian Labor Party

personality.temperament: He was a socialist newspaperman who had gone to prison for opposing conscription in 1916 and who, as prime minister, introduced it. He had fought drink and lost for years, then won. He walked the grounds of the Lodge at night during the Battle of the Coral Sea, unable to sleep. He told the country, in the week after Pearl Harbor, that Australia looked to America, free of any pangs about its links with Britain, and Churchill did not forgive him.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Perpetually on Guard, likes leaders who liberate cities and dislikes those who take cities from others; he brought Australia's divisions home to defend it.

history.bio: John Curtin was born in Creswick, Victoria, in 1885, left school at thirteen, and came up through the Victorian socialist movement and the timber workers' union. He edited the Westralian Worker in Perth, won Fremantle for Labor in 1928, and led the party from 1935. He became prime minister in October 1941 when two independents crossed the floor, and nine weeks later Japan entered the war. In December he turned to the United States over Britain's objection; in February 1942 he refused Churchill's order to divert the 7th Division to Burma and brought it home; he placed Australian forces under MacArthur's command, introduced conscription for service in the islands, and organised the economy for total war. His health broke under it. He died in office on 5 July 1945, six weeks before Japan's surrender. He is the only Australian prime minister to have died in the Lodge in wartime, and polls of historians regularly name him the country's greatest.
history.legacy: He turned Australia from Britain to America in a week and died before the war he directed was won.

civInfo.historical_background: John Curtin served as Australia's Prime Minister from 1941 to 1945, leading the country through the most direct existential threat it had faced: the Japanese advance through the Pacific during World War II, including air raids on Darwin and the fall of Singapore. Facing the limits of British support, Curtin controversially redirected Australian troops home from the Middle East and pivoted Australia's strategic alliance toward the United States, reshaping Australian foreign policy for the rest of the century. He died in office in July 1945, shortly before the war's end, worn down by the strain of wartime leadership. His defining legacy of turning a defensive crisis into national mobilization and a lasting policy of forming strong external alliances is reflected directly in his in-game kit's war-triggered production bonuses and preference for Defensive Pacts.

history.polity: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland; the British Empire
titles: Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

personality.temperament: She was eighteen and five feet tall when they woke her to tell her she was queen, and she asked to be left alone for an hour. She married her cousin Albert, bore nine children, and when he died at forty-two wore black for the remaining forty years. She disliked Gladstone and adored Disraeli, who made her an empress. She wrote two thousand five hundred words a day in her journal and most of Europe's royal houses descend from her. She reigned longer than any British monarch before her and the age took her name.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Sun Never Sets, likes leaders who settle on her continent and dislikes those who keep her from new ones; the empire covered a quarter of the land.

history.bio: Alexandrina Victoria was born at Kensington Palace in 1819 and succeeded her uncle William IV on 20 June 1837, the last of the Hanoverians in Britain. She married Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg in 1840 and governed with him, through the Chartists, the Irish famine, the Great Exhibition of 1851 and the Crimean War, until his death in December 1861. She withdrew from public life for a decade and the republican press grew; Disraeli drew her out and had her proclaimed Empress of India in 1876. Her reign saw the vote extended three times, the railways built, the Indian Mutiny and the Crown's assumption of India, the scramble for Africa and the Boer War. Her Golden and Diamond Jubilees in 1887 and 1897 were the empire's own festivals. She died at Osborne on 22 January 1901 at eighty-one, having reigned sixty-three years, with her grandson the German Kaiser at her bedside.
history.legacy: She reigned for sixty-three years over a quarter of the world and lent her name to the age.

civInfo.historical_background: Queen Victoria reigned over the United Kingdom from 1837 to 1901, a period that saw Britain become the dominant global industrial and colonial power, with an empire famously described as one 'on which the sun never sets.' Her reign coincided with the height of the Industrial Revolution -- steam-powered railways, factories, and the Royal Navy's coal-fired fleet all expanded dramatically during this era, which is exactly what this 'Age of Steam' persona's Industrial Zone and Strategic Resource bonuses represent. This persona (added via the Leader Pass's Rulers of England content) is a deliberately narrower, industrially-focused counterpart to the original 'Age of Empire' Victoria persona, whose ability and Redcoat unit instead modeled 19th-century British colonial expansion overseas.

dates.historicity: historical in Vietnamese tradition; Chinese sources are thin

history.polity: Jiuzhen (Cửu Chân) under the Chinese Wu dynasty, in what became Vietnam
titles: Nhụy Kiều Tướng quân (the Lady General Clad in Golden Robe)

personality.temperament: The Vietnamese tradition gives her a sentence that outlived her: that she would ride the storm, tread the waves, cut the whale from the eastern sea, sweep the frontier, and never bend her back to be a man's concubine. Chinese chroniclers called her a bandit and noted her height and her elephant. She refused marriage, refused her brother's caution and refused surrender.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Defender of the Homeland, likes leaders who hold their own lands and dislikes those who take cities from her; she fought one war, against an occupier.

history.bio: Triệu Thị Trinh was born in 225 CE in the district of Cửu Chân, in the Thanh Hóa country south of the Red River, under the rule of the Chinese state of Wu. Tradition says she killed a sister-in-law who abused her, went into the mountains, and gathered a thousand followers before she was twenty. In 248 she led a rising against the Wu governor, riding to battle on an elephant in yellow robes with a sword in each hand, and took the fortified towns of the district. Wu sent the general Lu Yin with eight thousand men. After several months of fighting her force broke, and she withdrew to Mount Tùng and died there, by her own hand according to the Vietnamese accounts. She was twenty-three. Later kings built her a temple and granted her posthumous titles, and her name was taken by Vietnamese nationalists for a thousand years of risings that came after.
history.legacy: She rose at twenty-three against the empire next door and set the pattern for every Vietnamese rising that followed.

quote.text: I want to ride the storm, tread the dangerous waves, win back the fatherland and destroy the yoke of slavery.
quote.source: Attributed in Vietnamese tradition; recorded in later chronicles, not in a contemporary source

civInfo.historical_background: Triệu Thị Trinh, known as Bà Triệu ('Lady Trieu'), was a 3rd-century CE Vietnamese woman who led an armed rebellion against occupying Chinese (Eastern Wu) rule around 248 CE. Vietnamese tradition holds she declared she would rather 'ride the wind and walk the waves' and fight as a warrior than live bowed under foreign rule as a servant, and though her rebellion was ultimately crushed, she became -- alongside the earlier Trung Sisters -- one of Vietnam's most enduring symbols of resistance to foreign domination. That legacy of guerrilla resistance fought from Vietnam's dense terrain against a more powerful invader directly informs her in-game kit, which rewards fighting from (and defending) Vietnam's woods, rainforest, and marsh tiles and never forgives a civilization that has declared war on her.

personality.temperament: The stelae of Naranjo show her standing on a bound captive, in the pose and dress of a king, and name her Ix Wak Chan Ajaw, Lady Six Sky. She came from Dos Pilas at nineteen to restart a dynasty that war had ended, never took the royal title, and ruled through a son she had at five years old crowned. For forty years the inscriptions record her wars. No other Maya woman left so many monuments.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Solitary, likes leaders who settle away from her and dislikes those who settle near her capital; Naranjo's wars were all with its neighbours.

history.bio: Wak Chanil Ajaw was a daughter of the king of Dos Pilas, a branch of the Tikal royal line allied to Calakmul, and in August 682 CE she arrived at Naranjo, a city in the Petén whose ruling house had been destroyed in war with Caracol. She took the government without the title of ajaw, performed the rituals of a king, and in 693 installed her five-year-old son K'ahk' Tiliw Chan Chaak on the throne. The monuments of the next decades record campaigns against Ucanal, Yaxha, Tuubal and others, a string of victories that rebuilt Naranjo's standing in the lowlands. Her stelae show her trampling captives, a pose otherwise reserved for male rulers, and record her bloodletting rites at the turning of the calendar. She outlived her son, who died in 728, and governed on into old age. Her last recorded date is 741. The Maya collapse took Naranjo within a century and a half of her death.
history.legacy: She rebuilt a destroyed kingdom from the throne she never claimed and left more monuments than any Maya queen.

leader_ability.name: Ix Mutal Ajaw
leader_ability.text: Within 6 tiles of her Capital, all of Lady Six Sky's units get bonus Combat Strength and her cities get a yield bonus, but any of her cities founded more than 6 tiles from the Capital instead take a yield penalty, strongly rewarding a small, tightly-clustered empire over a sprawling one.

agenda.name: Solitary
agenda.text: Lady Six Sky wants to keep her own cities clustered close together near her Capital; she likes leaders who settle far away from her and dislikes those who encroach on her borders.

civ_ability.name: Mayab
civ_ability.text: Mayan cities don't get the normal Housing bonus from being adjacent to fresh water or Coast, but their Farms grant bonus Housing and Gold instead (with an added Production bonus next to an Observatory), letting the Maya build tall, food-driven cities away from rivers.

unique_units.name: Hul'che
unique_units.notes: An Ancient-era ranged unit with higher Ranged Strength than the Archer and a bonus against already-wounded units, giving the Maya strong early skirmishing power, especially near the Capital where Lady Six Sky's ability adds further Combat Strength.

unique_infrastructure.name: Observatory
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Campus; gets a major Science bonus from each adjacent Plantation and a minor bonus from adjacent Farms or districts, tying neatly into the Maya's farm-focused civilization ability.

civInfo.historical_background: Lady Six Sky was a Maya queen who arrived at the city-state of Naranjo (in present-day Guatemala) around 682 CE and is credited with reviving it after a period of military defeat and decline, quite possibly having come from the powerful city of Dos Pilas or Calakmul. She oversaw military campaigns that restored Naranjo's regional power and, notably, placed her young son on the throne as king while continuing to wield significant authority herself, an unusual degree of female political power commemorated on Naranjo's carved stelae. That story of rebuilding and defending a single powerful city-state rather than pursuing distant conquest is mirrored directly in her in-game ability, which rewards a compact empire clustered tightly around the capital and penalizes overextension.

planSummary.one_line: Read the continent lens before the Settler plants, claim every site the home continent holds and nothing beyond it, and let Nkisi turn Relics, Artifacts and sculptures into Food, Production and Gold while half-again Great Artist and Musician points fill the Palace and the Theater Squares.

name: Nzinga Mbande
conditionCost: Continent-locked; overseas cities are actively bad
note: Same shape as Lady Six Sky but the ceiling is drawn by the map instead of a radius.

history.faith: Mbundu religion; baptised Catholic 1622, returned to the Church 1656

personality.temperament: At her first negotiation with the Portuguese governor in Luanda she was offered no chair, so a servant knelt and she sat on his back for the meeting. She was baptised when it helped, allied with the Dutch when it helped, led her soldiers in person into her sixties, and kept the Portuguese out of Matamba for thirty years. Her brother's murder, which she may have arranged, and the Imbangala alliance, with its sacrifices, are in the record beside the resistance.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Decolonization, likes leaders who keep their cities on their home continent and dislikes those who settle on hers; she fought Portugal's colony for forty years.

history.bio: Nzinga was born about 1583, a daughter of the ngola of Ndongo, a Mbundu kingdom inland from the Portuguese colony at Luanda. In 1622 she represented her brother at Luanda and negotiated a treaty that recognised Ndongo's independence; she was baptised Ana de Sousa there. When her brother died in 1624, by her hand according to some accounts, she took the throne. The Portuguese broke the treaty and drove her out in 1626; she allied with the Imbangala war bands, took the kingdom of Matamba in 1631, and from there fought Portugal for thirty years, allying with the Dutch during their occupation of Luanda from 1641 to 1648 and defeating a Portuguese army at Ngoleme in 1644. She made peace in 1656, returned to the Church with Capuchin missionaries at her court, and governed Matamba until her death in December 1663 at about eighty. Angola's independence movement took her as a founding figure three centuries later.
history.legacy: She held the Portuguese at the edge of Angola for forty years with every alliance the age offered, and died a queen at eighty.

terrain.why: Kongo's bias; Mbanza replaces the Neighborhood inside woods and rainforest
Chop nothing: the Mbanza needs the trees

affinity.barbarianStance: Cities on the home continent gain yields; the capital's neighbourhood is the empire. Clear camps on the home continent and let the rest be.

rivals.why: Philip cannot abide Kongo's refusal to found a religion

civInfo.name: Nzinga Mbande

leader_ability.name: Queen of Ndongo and Matamba
leader_ability.text: All Kongolese cities on the same continent as the Capital (including the Capital itself) get a bonus to all yields, while any cities founded on other continents instead suffer a yield penalty, strongly pushing Nzinga toward staying concentrated on her home continent rather than overseas colonization.

agenda.name: Decolonization
agenda.text: Nzinga favors civilizations that have not settled any cities on her home continent, and dislikes those that have established a foothold there, reflecting her historical resistance to foreign colonization.

civ_ability.name: Nkisi
civ_ability.text: Kongo gets bonus Food, Production, Faith, and Gold from Relics, Artifacts, and Sculptures (including Heroic Relics), earns Great Artist, Great Musician, and Great Merchant points faster, and its Palace can hold extra Great Works, making Kongo a strong Culture/Great Works-focused civilization.

unique_units.name: Ngao Mbeba
unique_units.notes: A stronger melee unit that avoids movement/sight penalties in Woods and Rainforest and gets a defensive bonus against ranged attacks, well suited to fighting through and defending Kongo's forested homeland.

unique_infrastructure.name: Mbanza
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Neighborhood; unlocked earlier (with Guilds instead of Urbanization) and grants Housing, Food, and Gold, but can only be built on Woods or Rainforest tiles, matching Kongo's historical jungle-based settlements.

civInfo.historical_background: Nzinga Mbande ruled the Central African kingdoms of Ndongo and later Matamba (in modern Angola) for roughly four decades in the 17th century, becoming one of the most formidable diplomats and military strategists to resist European colonization in her era. She skillfully played the Portuguese against rival African and Dutch powers, converted to Christianity as a political tool when useful, built alliances with escaped slaves and runaway soldiers to bolster her forces, and successfully kept her kingdoms independent of Portuguese control for most of her reign. Her lifelong struggle to keep foreign powers out of her home territory while she herself avoided overseas entanglement is the direct historical basis for her in-game ability and 'Decolonization' agenda, both of which reward staying concentrated on one's home continent and punish rivals who colonize it.

planSummary.one_line: Settle on hills, pin a Seowon two tiles out of every city with nothing ever built beside it and Mines and Farms all around it, pour every Governor title into promotions for Hwarang, and spend the early Science lead on a space race finished around turn 250, before rivals' adjacency catches up.

name: Seondeok
conditionCost: Seowon isolation forfeits all district adjacency stacking
note: Trades ceiling for floor. Guaranteed science on any start, but cannot be optimized upward.

personality.temperament: The Samguk Sagi gives her three prophecies: that a painted peony had no scent because the Chinese had sent no butterflies, that frogs croaking at a jade gate meant soldiers hiding in a valley, and the day of her own death. She built the oldest observatory still standing in East Asia and a nine-storey wooden pagoda meant to subdue nine enemies. A rebellion rose against her in her last year for being a woman; she died while it was being put down.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Cheomseongdae, likes leaders who invest in science and dislikes those who lag; she built an observatory before she built walls.

history.bio: Deokman was the eldest daughter of King Jinpyeong of Silla, who died in 632 without a son, and she succeeded him under the rule that only those of the sacred bone rank could reign. Silla was the smallest of the three Korean kingdoms and at war with both Baekje and Goguryeo; she sent students and envoys to Tang China, secured its alliance, and raised the general Kim Yu-sin and the statesman Kim Chunchu who would, under her successors, unify the peninsula. She built the Cheomseongdae observatory at Gyeongju, a bottle-shaped tower of 362 stones that still stands, the Hwangnyongsa nine-storey pagoda, the tallest wooden structure in Asia until the Mongols burned it, and the temple of Bunhwangsa. In 647 the noble Bidam rebelled, declaring that a woman could not rule; Kim Yu-sin crushed the rising, and Seondeok died in the same month, on the day she had foretold. Her cousin Jindeok, a second queen, followed her.
history.legacy: She ruled a kingdom at war with both its neighbours, built the oldest observatory in Asia, and set up the men who unified Korea.

terrain.why: The Seowon on a hill with no district beside it
Production for the Hwacha

affinity.barbarianStance: Korea builds science, not soldiers. Walls, one archer per city, and Hwacha later. Clear only what can see the capital.

civInfo.name: Seondeok

leader_ability.name: Hwarang
leader_ability.text: Each promotion a Governor has earned grants a percentage boost to both Culture and Science in the city they're assigned to, meaning heavily-promoted Governors turn into powerful Science and Culture engines under Seondeok.

agenda.name: Cheomseongdae
agenda.text: Seondeok focuses on maximizing her own empire's Science output and dislikes civilizations that produce comparatively little Science.

civ_ability.name: Three Kingdoms
civ_ability.text: Mines gain a Science yield and Farms gain a Food yield when placed adjacent to Korea's unique Seowon district, letting Korea weave its normal tile improvements directly into a Science-focused district strategy.

unique_units.name: Hwacha
unique_units.notes: A powerful Renaissance-era ranged siege unit that cannot move and attack in the same turn, trading mobility for strong ranged damage output.

unique_infrastructure.name: Seowon
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Campus and is Korea's central Science district, gaining adjacency bonuses from Mines and Farms placed near it rather than from the usual mountains/rainforest, tying directly into the Three Kingdoms civilization ability.

civInfo.historical_background: Seondeok reigned as Queen of Silla, one of Korea's Three Kingdoms, from 632 to 647 CE, becoming the first reigning queen in Korean history. Her rule is remembered for its patronage of Buddhism, learning, and science, including the construction of Cheomseongdae, widely regarded as the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in East Asia and the direct namesake of her in-game agenda. She also strengthened Silla's diplomatic ties with Tang China during a period of intense rivalry among Korea's Three Kingdoms, groundwork that helped Silla eventually unify the peninsula after her reign. Her hallmark blend of scholarly patronage, astronomy, and governance is reflected in her in-game kit's emphasis on Science output and Governor-driven yield bonuses.

planSummary.one_line: Trigger Eurekas instead of researching: each one is a whole technology, so chain them to Crossbowmen, Knights and Trebuchets by turn 80 and take the nearest neighbour's cities before turn 120. After that Babylon is a wide empire with half everyone else's Science, and it plays like one.

name: Hammurabi
conditionCost: Base per-turn Science permanently halved
note: The halving never goes away. Eureka availability thins in later eras, so the engine quietly dies.

dates.display: r. c. 1792 to c. 1750 BCE (middle chronology)

personality.temperament: His letters survive by the hundred, written to governors about canals, late taxes, a stolen ox and a bribed judge. He waited thirty years before making war on his rivals and then took them one by one. The stele of his laws shows him standing before the sun god, receiving the rod and ring of justice, and its prologue says he was called to make justice visible in the land so that the strong should not oppress the weak.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Cradle of Civilization, likes leaders who build and run many district types and dislikes those who build few; his laws governed every trade in Babylon.

history.bio: Hammurabi inherited Babylon in about 1792 BCE as one of a dozen Amorite kingdoms on the rivers of Mesopotamia, hemmed by Larsa, Eshnunna, Mari and Assyria. For three decades he dug canals, built walls and kept treaties. Then, in a span of about ten years from 1763, he beat Elam and Larsa, took Eshnunna, destroyed Mari, which had been his ally, and made Babylon the capital of all of Sumer and Akkad. His code of 282 laws, cut into a two-metre stele of black diorite near the end of his reign, set prices, wages, divorce terms, the liability of builders whose houses fell, and the lex talionis, an eye for an eye between equals and silver between unequals. The stele was carried off to Susa by the Elamites six centuries later and found there in 1901. His empire shrank under his son and was gone within a century and a half; the laws were copied in schools for a thousand years.
history.legacy: He wrote the oldest long code of law that survives and set it where everyone could read it.

terrain.why: River cities for the Palgum
Production to hard-build what Eurekas unlock early

naturalWonders.why: Great People to compensate for the science penalty

cityStates.why: Geneva and Taruga offset the Science malus
Production to build what Eurekas give

affinity.barbarianStance: Each Eureka completes its technology; killing a barbarian with a slinger, then an archer, is a free Archery and a free Machinery. Farm the first camp deliberately for Eurekas, then clear it.

civInfo.name: Hammurabi

leader_ability.name: Ninu Ilu Sirum
leader_ability.text: The first time each specialty district (except the Government Plaza) is constructed, Hammurabi instantly receives the lowest-production-cost building available for that district for free, plus a bonus Envoy for any other district built for the first time. This lets Babylon rush ahead on infrastructure and Eureka/Inspiration-style tech snowballing without spending production on the basic district buildings.

agenda.name: Cradle of Civilization
agenda.text: Hammurabi tries to build every possible type of district in his cities and respects civilizations that also pursue district variety; he looks down on civilizations that neglect districts.

civ_ability.name: Enuma Anu Enlil
civ_ability.text: Whenever Babylon triggers a Eureka or Inspiration, it can immediately unlock the full associated technology or civic by paying a share of its current per-turn Science or Culture output, letting a high-yield Babylon blitz through the tech/civic trees.

unique_units.name: Sabum Kibittum
unique_units.notes: An early melee unit with extra Movement and Sight and a large Combat Strength bonus against light and heavy cavalry, making it a strong early anti-horse defender.

unique_infrastructure.name: Palgum
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Water Mill; must be built in a city adjacent to a river, and adds Production, Housing, and extra Food from adjacent Freshwater tiles, reinforcing Babylon's strong early growth/science engine.

civInfo.historical_background: Hammurabi (r. c. 1792-1750 BCE) was the sixth king of the First Babylonian Dynasty, who unified much of Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule through a mix of diplomacy and conquest. He is best remembered for the Code of Hammurabi, one of the earliest and most complete written legal codes, inscribed on a stone stele and organized into numbered provisions ('ninu ilu sirum' loosely 'when the exalted god...' opens its prologue) that lend their name to his in-game ability. His reign also oversaw major irrigation and building projects along the Euphrates, echoed in Babylon's river-and-floodplain-focused kit and its free-district-building leader ability.

era_role.ancient_classical: Explosive. Eurekas convert to whole technologies.
era_role.medieval_renaissance: Eurekas thin out while the halved base science starts hurting.
era_role.industrial_modern: Actively behind. The penalty outlives the benefit.

guide_requirements: A Eureka availability audit per era, so the decline is visible before it bites.
A hard conversion deadline: the tech lead must become military, wonders, or territory by a set point.
An explicit late-game plan that assumes a science deficit rather than a lead.

template.principle: The ability has an expiry. The guide is a timer wrapped around a conversion deadline. Its most important content is not the build order, it is the turn the plan stops and what replaces it.

structure.goal: Reach the window with everything already staged. Nothing in this phase is optional; staging done after the window opens is spent from the budget.
steps: Turn 1: identify the target. Hammurabi's window is short enough that target selection cannot wait for scouting to finish.
Turns 1-15: scout toward the target only. Exploration away from the target is a luxury this shape cannot afford.
Turns 10-30: production goes to the units or charges the window will consume. Infrastructure that pays back after 120 is deferred.
Pre-window checkpoint: confirm the condition is met: Base per-turn Science permanently halved, and that units are within striking distance, not at home.

structure.goal: Convert tempo into permanent assets. Cities, wonders, or improvements. Not kills, not gold, not map presence.
core_loop: Each turn, ask: is the objective closer than it was last turn?
If the answer is no for three consecutive turns, the window is failing. Go to the abort branch.
Track remaining turns explicitly. The player should always know the number.

checkpoints.test: Is at least half the objective secured?
checkpoints.if_no: Reduce scope now. Take one city instead of three. Partial conversion beats total expiry.

checkpoints.test: Has the tempo become something permanent?

structure.goal: Stabilize what was taken. This phase is longer than both prior phases combined and most guides for this shape underwrite it badly.
steps: Amenity and loyalty audit on every acquired city before any new construction.
Infrastructure catch-up: the arming phase deliberately skipped this, and the bill comes due now.
Choose a victory path. From here the era leads and the kit follows. Actively behind. The penalty outlives the benefit.

abort_branch.trigger: Window closed with no permanent gain, or three stalled turns before the midpoint.
actions: Make peace immediately. Prolonging a failed window converts a bad position into a lost game.
Disband surplus units. The maintenance is now pure loss.
Switch to the generic development plan for the empire you actually have.

template.fail_state: The window closed and nothing permanent was gained. Hammurabi is now an ordinary civ with an army it cannot afford and grievances it cannot repay.
anti_patterns: Writing Phase 3 as an afterthought. It is most of the game.
Expressing the deadline as a turn number only. Tie it to opponent tech where possible, since that is what actually closes the window.
Letting the player believe a large army at 120 counts as success. It does not.

planSummary.one_line: Count the luxuries before you count the land, settle only as many cities as you can keep Ecstatic, and let Scottish Enlightenment turn every Campus and Industrial Zone into a doubled Great Scientist and Great Engineer mint. Bannockburn is a ten-turn Production burst you take once, if a neighbour hands you the cause.

name: Robert the Bruce
conditionCost: Permanent Ecstatic amenity upkeep across the whole empire
note: The bonus is rented every single turn. One luxury loss switches it off empire-wide.

personality.temperament: He changed sides three times in the wars with Edward I before he killed his rival John Comyn at the altar of Greyfriars in Dumfries and had himself crowned six weeks later. He lost two battles in a year, lost three brothers to the executioner, and spent a winter in hiding, where the spider is said to have taught him to try again. He won by burning castles rather than holding them and by choosing the one battle he could win. He died of leprosy, or something like it, and asked that his heart be carried to the Holy Land.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Flower of Scotland, dislikes leaders who declare war on his neighbours and will fight for them; he spent his reign fighting for one.

history.bio: Robert Bruce was born in 1274, heir to the earldom of Carrick and the Bruce claim to the Scottish throne that Edward I of England had rejected in favour of John Balliol. He served Edward, then Wallace, then Edward again. On 10 February 1306 he met John Comyn, his rival claimant, in the church of the Greyfriars at Dumfries and killed him, and on 25 March was crowned at Scone. He was beaten at Methven and Dalry that summer and fled to the western isles while Edward hanged his supporters and imprisoned his wife and daughter. From 1307 he fought a guerrilla war, recovered the north, and razed every castle he took. Edward I died marching against him. On 23 and 24 June 1314 at Bannockburn he destroyed Edward II's army, twice his size, in the marshes below Stirling. The Declaration of Arbroath in 1320 told the pope that Scotland would never be subject to England; the treaty of Edinburgh in 1328 made England agree. He died at Cardross in June 1329.
history.legacy: He took a crown by murder, lost everything, and won it back at Bannockburn so completely that England signed.

terrain.why: Golf Courses and happy cities on hills
Scotland's historical coast

affinity.barbarianStance: Scotland's science comes from happy cities, and a raided city is not happy. Walls early, Highlanders much later; clear the camps within sight and leave the rest.

civInfo.name: Robert the Bruce

leader_ability.name: Bannockburn
leader_ability.text: Once Scotland researches the Defensive Tactics civic, Robert can declare a War of Liberation; doing so grants all his units +100% Production and +2 Movement for the following 10 turns, turning a defensive liberation war into a powerful offensive window.

agenda.name: Flower of Scotland
agenda.text: Robert will not attack civilizations that share a landmass with him unless they break a promise, and he dislikes leaders who attack their own neighbors unprovoked.

civ_ability.name: Scottish Enlightenment
civ_ability.text: Happy cities gain bonus Science and Production, plus extra Great Scientist points per Campus and Great Engineer points per Industrial Zone; Ecstatic cities double these bonuses, rewarding Scotland for maximizing city Amenities.

unique_units.name: Highlander
unique_units.notes: A Recon-class unit that fights especially well in Hills and Woods, well suited to Scotland's rugged, resource-rich terrain.

unique_infrastructure.name: Golf Course
unique_infrastructure.notes: A unique tile improvement that generates Amenities and Gold once built, rewarding Scotland's happiness-driven playstyle.

civInfo.historical_background: Robert the Bruce (1274-1329) was King of Scots who led Scotland during the Wars of Scottish Independence against England. His decisive victory at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314 secured effective Scottish independence and is the namesake of his signature in-game ability, which rewards declaring a liberating war. Earlier in his career he had also endured defeats and exile before rallying Scottish nobles to his cause, reflecting the game's framing of him as a defensive, promise-keeping leader who only turns aggressive when wronged.

planSummary.one_line: Settle beside mountains, woods and coast, never chop, mine or dig a quarry where it lowers Appeal, let the Breathtaking tiles pay Science and Culture from turn 20, decide by turn 60 whether the Culture goes to Tourism or the Wildcard Favor goes to the World Congress, and close with National Parks, Film Studios and Rock Bands.

name: Teddy Roosevelt
conditionCost: Cannot chop; forfeits the standard production-acceleration lever
note: Appeal is a permanent tile property, so the yields never decay.

dates.display: President of the United States 1901 to 1909

personality.temperament: He was an asthmatic child who built his body by will, a rancher, a police commissioner, a historian, a colonel who charged up a hill in Cuba, and a president at forty-two because an anarchist shot the one before him. He broke trusts, dug a canal, sent a fleet around the world, won a Nobel Prize for ending a war, and set aside 230 million acres of the public land. He was shot in the chest in 1912 and gave the speech anyway. He wanted to be in every fight, and he usually was.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Big Stick, likes leaders who keep the peace on his continent and dislikes those who start wars on it; the Roosevelt Corollary claimed the hemisphere.

history.bio: Theodore Roosevelt was born in New York in 1858, entered the state assembly at twenty-three, lost his wife and mother on the same day in 1884, and went to the Dakota Badlands to ranch. He came back to reform the civil service and the New York police, resigned from the Navy Department in 1898 to raise the Rough Riders, and rode up San Juan Heights into the governorship of New York and the vice-presidency. McKinley's assassination made him president in September 1901. He broke up Northern Securities, mediated the coal strike, took Panama and began the canal, brokered the peace between Russia and Japan at Portsmouth, and used the Antiquities Act and the Forest Service to protect more land than any president before or since, including five national parks. He left office in 1909, hunted in Africa, split the Republicans in 1912 as a Progressive, took a bullet in the chest in Milwaukee and finished his speech, explored an unmapped river in Brazil, and died in his sleep in January 1919.
history.legacy: He made the presidency a bully pulpit and the national parks a national habit, and he never once stood still.

quote.text: Speak softly and carry a big stick; you will go far.
quote.source: Speech at the Minnesota State Fair, 2 September 1901, quoting what he called a West African proverb

terrain.why: Appeal for National Parks and the Rough Rider bonus on the home continent
Appeal and production
Film Studios in big cities

affinity.barbarianStance: Units on the home continent get +5 strength; camps on it are easy. Clear everything on the home continent, ignore everything off it.

civInfo.name: Teddy Roosevelt (Bull Moose)

leader_ability.name: Antiquities and Parks (Bull Moose persona of Roosevelt Corollary)
leader_ability.text: The default (non-persona) Teddy Roosevelt's ability, Roosevelt Corollary, grants units +5 Combat Strength on his home continent and +1 Appeal to all tiles in any city containing a National Park. When Persona Packs are enabled, Roosevelt splits into two alternate personas: Rough Rider (keeps a Roosevelt Corollary variant focused on the home-continent combat bonus and doubled Envoys to trade-route city-states) and Bull Moose, whose ability 'Antiquities and Parks' instead grants bonus Science on tiles of Breathtaking Appeal adjacent to a Natural Wonder or Mountain, and bonus Culture on Breathtaking tiles adjacent to a Wonder or Woods — a peaceful, conservation-and-culture playstyle built around National Parks and high-Appeal terrain.

agenda.name: Big Stick Policy
agenda.text: Roosevelt (in both personas) likes peaceful civilizations that share his continent and dislikes any civilization that starts a war on that continent.

civ_ability.name: Founding Fathers
civ_ability.text: America's civilization ability has evolved across versions: in the base game it halved the time to earn government legacy bonuses; in Rise and Fall it instead converts all Diplomatic policy slots in the current government into Wildcard slots; Gathering Storm added +1 Diplomatic Favor per turn for each Wildcard slot in the current government, making America's policy setup unusually flexible.

unique_units.name: Rough Rider
unique_units.notes: An Industrial era heavy cavalry unit with a Combat Strength bonus on Hills and reduced maintenance, reflecting Roosevelt's historical cavalry regiment.

unique_units.name: P-51 Mustang
unique_units.notes: A Modern era air unit with bonus attack against other fighters, extra range, and faster experience gain, giving America strong air superiority in the late game.

unique_infrastructure.name: Film Studio
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Broadcast Center and adds extra Tourism pressure toward other civilizations in the Modern era, supporting a Culture/Tourism victory.

civInfo.historical_background: Theodore 'Teddy' Roosevelt (1858-1919) was the 26th U.S. President, a Progressive-era reformer known for trust-busting, conservation of public lands, and an assertive foreign policy summarized by his phrase 'speak softly and carry a big stick' (the source of his in-game agenda name). After leaving the presidency he ran for a third term in 1912 as the candidate of the Progressive 'Bull Moose' Party, the persona referenced in this leader's parenthetical name, campaigning on social reform rather than the more militaristic image of his earlier 'Rough Rider' cavalry service in the Spanish-American War. His dual legacy as both war hero and national-parks conservationist is split directly into Civ VI's two Roosevelt personas.

name: Kupe
conditionCost: No chopping, plus an ocean start with no immediate settle
note: Pays a real opening tempo cost before the ramp begins.

dates.historicity: legendary; the settlement of Aotearoa c. 1250 to 1300 is historical

history.polity: Hawaiki (the ancestral Polynesian homeland); Aotearoa (New Zealand)

personality.temperament: The traditions differ by iwi, but they agree on the ocean. He left Hawaiki in the canoe Matahourua, chasing a great octopus that had stolen his people's bait, or fleeing a quarrel over a woman, and found a long white cloud on the horizon that his wife named Aotearoa. He sailed its coasts and named its places, Castlepoint, Mana, the Hokianga where he turned for home. He went back to Hawaiki with the sailing directions. He did not return.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Kaitiakitanga, likes leaders who keep their land's appeal high and dislikes those who strip it; his descendants are the guardians of the land he found.

history.bio: Kupe is the navigator credited in many Māori traditions with the discovery of Aotearoa. The stories place his homeland in Hawaiki, the ancestral land of Polynesian memory, and give him a double-hulled voyaging canoe, the Matahourua, a wife Kuramārōtini, and a companion or rival, Ngake. He is said to have followed the long-tailed cuckoo south, found the islands empty of people, named the coasts and the harbours, fought the octopus of Muturangi in Cook Strait, and sailed home with the star path, the Hokianga-nui-a-Kupe, the great returning place of Kupe, marking where he left. Later voyages of the great fleet followed his directions. Archaeology dates the first settlement of New Zealand to about 1250 to 1300 CE, the last large landmass on Earth to be settled by people, and the wayfinding by stars, swells and birds that the tradition describes is how it was done. Kupe's name is on the land in a dozen places and on no stone.
history.legacy: He found the last empty land on Earth and left the directions so that others could.

terrain.why: The Marae and fishing boats; appeal on every shore
Woods give production and the Māori cannot harvest them
Unimproved rainforest yields extra for the Māori

affinity.barbarianStance: Kupe lands late and alone; the first camp near the landing is the first threat. Toa warriors clear it; after that, keep ships on patrol and let inland camps be.

civInfo.name: Kupe

leader_ability.name: Kupe's Voyage
leader_ability.text: Kupe begins the game embarked on the Ocean rather than on land, earning +2 Science and +2 Culture per turn before he founds his first city. Founding that first city grants a free Builder and +1 Population, and his Palace provides extra Housing and an Amenity, smoothing the unusual late, ocean-based start.

agenda.name: Kaitiakitanga
agenda.text: Kupe preserves natural features and builds National Parks; he likes civilizations that respect the environment (avoiding harvesting and terrain removal) and dislikes those who despoil it.

civ_ability.name: Mana
civ_ability.text: The Māori start with Sailing and Shipbuilding and can move directly onto Ocean tiles from the outset. Their embarked units gain bonus Combat Strength and Movement, unimproved Woods and Rainforest tiles yield bonus Production, and Fishing Boats grant extra Food and trigger a Culture Bomb, making the Māori strong at settling and expanding across open ocean.

unique_units.name: Toa
unique_units.notes: A Classical era melee unit that can build the defensive Pā improvement on hills and weakens adjacent enemy units with a Haka war dance, giving the Māori solid mid-game defense despite their peaceful, exploration-focused kit.

unique_infrastructure.name: Marae
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Amphitheater in the Theater Square; it grants Culture and Faith from every passable feature (e.g., Woods, Floodplains) in the city and Tourism after Flight, rewarding a Māori empire that keeps its natural terrain intact.

civInfo.historical_background: Kupe is a legendary Polynesian navigator credited in Māori oral tradition with being one of the first explorers to discover and name Aotearoa (New Zealand), guiding a great ocean-going waka (canoe) across the Pacific using wayfinding by stars, currents, and birds. As a figure of oral history rather than documented record, his exact dates are unknown, but he is central to Māori foundational narratives of migration and settlement. His in-game role as an ocean-starting leader who arrives to found cities directly mirrors this voyaging legend, and the Māori civilization's environmental, ocean-adjacency-focused kit reflects traditional Māori concepts of kaitiakitanga (guardianship of nature).

name: Pericles
conditionCost: Ongoing envoy investment; suzerainty can be taken from you
note: Flat and smooth, but rented. Losing suzerainty is an instant global culture cut.

dates.display: leading statesman of Athens c. 461 to 429 BCE

history.polity: Athenian democracy and the Delian League

personality.temperament: Thucydides, who heard him, said Athens under him was in name a democracy and in fact the rule of its first citizen. He was elected general fifteen years running and never took a bribe. He kept one friend's circle, Anaxagoras, Phidias, Aspasia, and spoke in public rarely, so that each speech landed. The comic poets called him the onion-head for the shape of his skull and the Olympian for his thunder. He buried two sons in the plague before it took him.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Delian League, likes leaders who leave the city-states he holds alone and dislikes those who compete for them; the League was Athens' empire.

history.bio: Pericles was born around 495 BCE to Xanthippus, the victor of Mycale, and Agariste of the Alcmaeonid house. He entered politics in the 460s, prosecuted Cimon, backed the reforms of Ephialtes that stripped the Areopagus, and after Ephialtes was murdered in 461 led the democratic party for thirty years. He had the citizens paid for jury service, limited citizenship to those born of two Athenians, moved the treasury of the Delian League from Delos to Athens in 454 and spent it on the Parthenon, the Propylaea and the Odeon. He made peace with Persia and a thirty-year truce with Sparta, planted colonies, and put down Samos. When the truce broke in 431 he brought the whole population inside the Long Walls and let Attica burn, trusting the fleet. The plague of 430 killed a quarter of the city, including his sons; the assembly fined him, re-elected him, and in 429 the plague killed him. The war he started lasted twenty-seven years and Athens lost it.
history.legacy: He led Athens for thirty years, built the Parthenon with the League's money, and began the war that ended Athenian power.

quote.text: Our constitution is called a democracy because power is in the hands not of a minority but of the whole people.
quote.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.37, the Funeral Oration

civInfo.name: Pericles

agenda.name: Delian League

civ_ability.name: Plato's Republic

unique_units.name: Hoplite

unique_infrastructure.name: Acropolis

civInfo.historical_background: Pericles (c. 495-429 BCE) was the leading statesman of Athens during its Golden Age, guiding the city through the height of its democratic institutions, its cultural flourishing (including the Parthenon and other Acropolis monuments, echoed by Greece's unique district), and the early years of the Peloponnesian War against Sparta. He was famously eulogized by Thucydides as effectively Athens' 'first citizen' despite holding no monarchical title, a nod reflected in his in-game leader title. His policy of forging and managing an alliance network among Greek city-states — the Delian League — is the direct inspiration for his in-game agenda's focus on city-state suzerainty.

planSummary.one_line: Settle every city on a river with Floodplains in its first ring, build wonders and districts on the Floodplains at river speed, and decide by turn 70 whether the Appeal the Floodplains now give becomes a National Park and Seaside Resort Culture game or a Campus-in-every-river-city Science game.

name: Cleopatra
conditionCost: River and floodplain dependency
note: Appeal inversion pays early in Food and late in National Parks. Genuinely two-phase.

personality.temperament: Plutarch said her beauty was not remarkable but her voice and conversation were, and that she spoke Egyptian, which no Ptolemy before her had bothered to learn, along with Greek, Ethiopian, Hebrew, Arabic, Syriac, Median and Parthian. She chose her allies among the most powerful men alive and bore their children. When the last alliance failed she chose her own death over a Roman triumph.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Queen of the Nile, likes leaders with strong militaries and dislikes weak ones; she allied with Caesar and Antony because each was the strongest man in Rome.

history.bio: Cleopatra VII Philopator was born in 69 BCE, the daughter of Ptolemy XII, in a Greek dynasty that had ruled Egypt since Alexander's general took it. She became queen in 51 BCE beside her brother, lost a civil war to him, and in 48 had herself carried into Caesar's quarters in Alexandria rolled in a carpet or a bedroll; the brother drowned in the Nile and she ruled. She bore Caesar a son, Caesarion, and lived in Rome until Caesar was killed. In 41 she met Mark Antony at Tarsus, sailing up the Cydnus in a gilded barge, and over ten years bore him three children and bound Egypt's treasury to his half of the Roman world. Octavian defeated them at Actium in 31 BCE. Antony fell on his sword; Cleopatra, taken in her mausoleum, died in August 30 BCE, by an asp in the tradition and by poison in all likelihood. Egypt became a Roman province. She was the last pharaoh.
history.legacy: She was the last ruler of independent Egypt, and she chose the manner of its ending.

terrain.why: Egypt builds districts and wonders on floodplains and takes no flood damage
Sphinxes and Desert Folklore turn the sand to faith and culture
River grassland for the growth the floodplains start

pantheons.why: Production from floodplains, the Egyptian engine
Wonders 15% faster on top of Iteru

cityStates.why: Trade routes to Egypt pay her and her partner

affinity.barbarianStance: Egypt's Maryannu Chariot Archers run down raiders on open floodplains; use them to clear the two nearest camps and then park them. Wonders are the plan, not camps.

civInfo.name: Cleopatra (Ptolemaic)
civInfo.expansion_origin: New Frontier Pass (Persona Packs) for the base 'Cleopatra' persona; Ptolemaic Cleopatra specifically is a Leader Pass persona (Rulers of the Sahara Pack)

leader_ability.name: Arrival of Hapi
leader_ability.text: As the Ptolemaic persona (added later via the Leader Pass' Rulers of the Sahara Pack), Cleopatra's ability grants resources on Floodplains +1 Food and +1 Culture, and Floodplains in her territory grant adjacent tiles +1 Appeal instead of the usual -1. (Her original, base-game persona instead uses the ability Mediterranean's Bride, which gives bonus Gold on Egypt's outgoing Trade Routes and bonus Food/Gold on incoming ones.)

agenda.name: Basilike Ge
agenda.text: As Ptolemaic Cleopatra, she favors civilizations with high Food output and dislikes those with low Food output. (Her original persona's agenda, Queen of the Nile, instead favors leaders with powerful militaries and dislikes weak ones.)

civ_ability.name: Iteru
civ_ability.text: Egypt builds Wonders and districts faster when adjacent to a river, and uniquely can construct Wonders and districts directly on Floodplains, letting Egypt turn its floodplain-heavy river valleys into dense wonder- and district-packed cities.

unique_units.name: Maryannu Chariot Archer
unique_units.notes: A fast Ancient era ranged cavalry unit with strong Ranged Strength and extra Movement on open terrain, giving Egypt an unusually powerful early rush/exploration unit.

unique_infrastructure.name: Sphinx
unique_infrastructure.notes: A unique tile improvement giving Faith and Culture (with a bonus when adjacent to a Wonder), and Tourism after Flight, reinforcing Egypt's wonder- and culture-focused playstyle.

civInfo.historical_background: Cleopatra VII Thea Philopator (69-30 BCE) was the last active ruler of Egypt's Ptolemaic dynasty, a Greek Macedonian line established after Alexander the Great's conquests, ruling Egypt for nearly three centuries before Roman annexation. Fluent, politically astute, and famed for her alliances with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, she worked to preserve Egyptian independence against expanding Roman power, ultimately losing at the Battle of Actium. Civ VI splits her into two personas reflecting this hybrid identity: a base-game 'Egyptian' Cleopatra evoking the older pharaonic tradition and river/floodplain economy of the Nile, and a Leader Pass 'Ptolemaic' persona (Arrival of Hapi, named for the Egyptian god of the Nile flood) emphasizing her Hellenistic-Egyptian royal household and its farmland (basilike ge, 'royal land').

name: Pedro II
conditionCost: Rainforest dependency; must not clear it
note: Great People refunds compound. Every recruit makes the next one cheaper in real terms.

personality.temperament: He became emperor at five when his father sailed for Portugal, and he was crowned at fourteen because the regents could not keep order. He spoke a dozen languages, corresponded with Darwin, Pasteur and Victor Hugo, sat in the front row at Wagner's Bayreuth, and visited Alexander Graham Bell's stall at Philadelphia and said, my God, it talks. He freed the slaves by proxy and was deposed by the army a year later. He died in a Paris hotel with a pillow of Brazilian earth.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Magnanimous, likes leaders who recruit Great People and does not begrudge them; he spent his reign among scientists and poets.

history.bio: Pedro de Alcântara was born in Rio de Janeiro in December 1825 and became emperor of Brazil in April 1831 at the age of five when his father, Pedro I, abdicated. A troubled regency ended with his early majority in 1840. For the next forty-nine years he governed a constitutional monarchy larger than Europe, with a parliament, a free press and a court that imported science and opera; he founded institutes, schools and observatories and travelled abroad three times, the first Brazilian ruler to do so. He fought Paraguay in the War of the Triple Alliance from 1864 to 1870 at great cost. He pushed the abolition of slavery by degrees, the free womb law of 1871 and the Golden Law of 1888 signed by his daughter Isabel while he was in Europe. The planters who had lost their slaves and the officers who wanted a republic deposed him on 15 November 1889; he went into exile without resistance and died in Paris in December 1891. Brazil brought his body home in 1921.
history.legacy: He ruled Brazil for half a century as a scholar-emperor, ended slavery, and was sent into exile for it.

civInfo.historical_background: Dom Pedro II (1825-1891) ruled the Empire of Brazil for nearly 50 years, presiding over a long period of relative internal stability, gradual abolition of slavery, and active patronage of the sciences and arts (he corresponded with scientists worldwide and funded research and exhibitions), which inspires his in-game focus on collecting Great People. His reign ended with a bloodless 1889 military coup that established the Brazilian republic, after which he lived out his life in exile in Europe. Brazil's unusual rainforest-friendly civilization ability reflects the country's Amazonian geography, a defining feature of the empire he ruled.

history.polity: Kingdom of Bavaria (within the German Empire from 1871)

personality.temperament: He came to the throne at eighteen, tall and handsome, and within weeks had summoned Wagner, whose debts he paid and whose operas he staged for himself alone. He withdrew from Munich and from people, slept by day, drove through the mountains at night in a gilded sleigh, and built castles he never finished and could not afford: Neuschwanstein on its crag, Linderhof with its grotto, Herrenchiemsee copied from Versailles. His ministers had him declared insane. He drowned in a lake the next day with the doctor who had certified him.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Dreamer of the Mountain, likes leaders who build wonders and dislikes those who let their cities fall into disrepair; he built three castles and bankrupted himself.

history.bio: Ludwig became king of Bavaria in March 1864 on his father's sudden death. He was eighteen, unprepared, and devoted to Richard Wagner, whom he brought to Munich and financed through Tristan, Die Meistersinger and the building of Bayreuth. Bavaria fought on Austria's side in 1866 and lost; in 1870 Ludwig's letter proposing the Prussian king as German emperor, written at Bismarck's dictation in exchange for a secret pension, made Bavaria a state within the German Empire. He withdrew from government and from the capital. From 1869 he built Neuschwanstein, from 1874 Linderhof, from 1878 Herrenchiemsee, borrowing against the civil list until his debts reached fourteen million marks and his ministers, fearing he would sell Bavaria to pay them, had him deposed as insane on 10 June 1886. On 13 June he was found dead in the shallows of Lake Starnberg with Dr Gudden, his examiner. The castles he built on credit are now Bavaria's largest source of tourist income.
history.legacy: He ruined a treasury on castles for an audience of one, and the castles now pay for Bavaria.

terrain.why: Production for wonders

affinity.barbarianStance: Ludwig builds castles, not armies. Walls first, Discipline, and clear the nearest camp with the Hansa-funded warriors before the first wonder.

civInfo.historical_background: Ludwig II (1845-1886) was King of Bavaria, famous less for statecraft than for his extravagant, fairy-tale castle-building projects — most notably Neuschwanstein Castle — and his devoted patronage of composer Richard Wagner, which together earned him the nickname 'the Swan King,' the name of his in-game ability. His reign saw Bavaria's political independence curtailed as Germany unified under Prussian leadership, and he died in disputed circumstances shortly after being declared mentally unfit to rule. As a Leader Pass persona representing Germany despite historically ruling only Bavaria, his in-game focus on wonder-building and culture/tourism is a direct nod to his architectural obsessions.

name: Kristina
conditionCost: None mechanically, but no early-game identity at all
note: Auto-theming is pure late-game convenience. Needs a survival plan for the first 80 turns.

titles: Duchess of Estonia, Livonia and Karelia

personality.temperament: She was raised as a prince because her father ordered it, rode and shot and swore like one, and read ten hours a day. She brought Descartes to Stockholm and he died of the winter. She would not marry, would not stay Lutheran and would not stay queen; she abdicated at twenty-seven, rode to Rome in men's clothes, converted, and spent the rest of her life collecting paintings, manuscripts and debts. She is one of four women buried in St Peter's.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Minerva of the North, likes leaders with many Great Works and wonders and dislikes those with few; she stripped Prague's castle for her library.

history.bio: Christina was born in Stockholm in December 1626, the only surviving child of Gustavus Adolphus, who was killed at Lützen when she was six. She was educated as a king's heir and took the government in 1644 at eighteen, during the last years of the Thirty Years' War, which the Peace of Westphalia ended in 1648 with Sweden a great power. She made her court a university, bringing Descartes, Grotius, Salmasius and Vossius to Stockholm and filling the castle with the libraries and galleries her armies had taken from Prague. In June 1654 she abdicated in favour of her cousin Charles Gustav, left Sweden within days, and in 1655 was received into the Catholic Church at Innsbruck. She settled in Rome, founded the academy that became the Arcadia, patronised Scarlatti and Corelli and Bernini, intrigued for the crowns of Naples and Poland, and had her equerry Monaldeschi executed at Fontainebleau for betraying her. She died in Rome in 1689.
history.legacy: She gave up a crown to keep her mind her own and made Rome's greatest private collection with Sweden's spoils.

terrain.why: Growth for the Great Works the Queen's Bibliotheque holds
Production for the Open-Air Museum

pantheons.why: Production from the Nobel economy's mines

affinity.barbarianStance: Sweden has no early military edge. Walls and one archer per city; clear camps only when they threaten a Theater Square.

civInfo.name: Kristina

leader_ability.name: Minerva of the North

agenda.name: Bibliophile
agenda.text: Kristina tries to collect as many Great Works as possible and likes leaders who leave Great Works for her to acquire; she dislikes rivals who compete hard for the same Great Works.

civ_ability.name: Nobel Prize
civ_ability.text: Sweden gains bonus Great Scientist and Great Engineer points from Universities and Factories, generates Diplomatic Favor for every Great Person it recruits, and unlocks three unique World Congress competitions from the Industrial era onward, blending science, culture, and diplomacy.

unique_units.name: Carolean
unique_units.notes: A Renaissance era unit with extra Movement and a Combat Strength bonus for each point of unused Movement, plus bonus strength against cavalry, rewarding aggressive, mobile play.

unique_infrastructure.name: Open-Air Museum
unique_infrastructure.notes: Grants Culture and Tourism scaling with the variety of terrain types (Snow, Tundra, Desert, Plains, Grassland) Swedish cities are founded on, up to one per city, rewarding geographically diverse settling.

civInfo.historical_background: Kristina (1626-1689) was Queen of Sweden from 1632 to 1654, a famously erudite and unconventional monarch who turned Stockholm into a hub for scholars, philosophers (including René Descartes, who died there), and artists, earning Sweden the nickname 'Athens of the North' during her reign — the direct inspiration for her in-game 'Minerva of the North' ability and Great Works focus. She abdicated the throne in 1654, converted to Catholicism (a controversial act for a Lutheran monarch), and spent much of her later life in Rome as a patron of the arts and sciences. Her personal passion for collecting books, art, and manuscripts is reflected in Sweden's Great Works/Bibliophile-centered kit.

name: Catherine de Medici
conditionCost: None
note: Rare kit that pays in every era for a different reason: spy, then combat visibility, then tourism.

dates.display: Queen consort 1547 to 1559; regent and queen mother to 1589

personality.temperament: She was orphaned at three weeks, held hostage in a convent during the siege of Florence, and married at fourteen to a prince who preferred his mistress for twenty-five years. She waited. When her husband died she governed through three sons, balancing Catholic and Huguenot factions that each wanted the other dead, and she spent what the treasury did not have on festivals, ballets and palaces. Her enemies made her a poisoner; the record makes her a survivor.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Black Queen, favours leaders with strong intelligence networks and distrusts those who keep none; she ran the most elaborate court of spies in Europe.

history.bio: Caterina de' Medici was born in Florence in 1519, the last legitimate heir of the elder Medici line, and was married at fourteen to Henri, second son of Francis I of France, in a bargain between the French crown and her uncle Pope Clement VII. She bore ten children after a decade of barrenness. Henri II died in a tournament in 1559 and she governed for three sons in succession, Francis II, Charles IX and Henri III, through the Wars of Religion. She tried toleration first, at Saint-Germain in 1562, and failed. In August 1572, days after her daughter's wedding to the Protestant Henri of Navarre, Paris murdered thousands of Huguenots in the Saint Bartholomew's Day massacre; how far she ordered it is still argued, and she did not stop it. She built the Tuileries, bought Chenonceau, commissioned Nostradamus and Ronsard, and died in January 1589 eight months before her last son was stabbed to death.
history.legacy: She held the French crown together through thirty years of civil war and three weak kings, at a price Paris still remembers.

(Her alternate Magnificence persona instead focuses on collecting and trading Luxury resources via the agenda 'Sumptuous Finery.')

civInfo.historical_background: Catherine de' Medici (1519-1589) was an Italian-born queen consort and later regent of France during the tumultuous French Wars of Religion, wielding influence over her sons' reigns as king. She earned a fearsome reputation — fairly or not — for court intrigue, poison plots, and involvement in events like the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre, cementing the 'Black Queen' legend that names her default in-game persona and its espionage/spy focus. Her family's Medici banking and political dynasty in Florence also connects to her later New Frontier persona, 'Magnificence,' which instead emphasizes courtly luxury and the collection of fine resources, echoing the opulent Medici court culture.

conditionCost: Tundra start; the terrain bonus is survival, not growth

titles: Knight Grand Cross of St Michael and St George

personality.temperament: He called it the sunny way, the policy of persuasion over coercion, and he used it for fifteen years to hold a country of two languages and two faiths together through a school crisis, a South African war and a naval bill. He was the first French Canadian prime minister and the first to be knighted. He said the twentieth century would belong to Canada and filled the prairies to make it true. He lost power over free trade with the United States and died still leading the opposition.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, The Last Best West, likes leaders who settle tundra and dislikes those who ignore it; he settled the prairies with a million immigrants.

history.bio: Henri-Charles-Wilfrid Laurier was born at Saint-Lin, Canada East, in 1841, trained in law at McGill, and entered the Commons in 1874. He led the Liberal Party from 1887, won the 1896 election on the Manitoba Schools question, and governed for fifteen years, the longest unbroken term in Canadian history. His immigration minister Clifford Sifton opened the prairies to two million settlers from Britain, the United States and eastern Europe; Alberta and Saskatchewan became provinces in 1905; the Grand Trunk Pacific was begun; the wheat economy was built. He sent volunteers, not conscripts, to the Boer War, created a Canadian navy in 1910 that satisfied neither the imperialists nor the Quebec nationalists, and in 1911 lost the election over reciprocity, a free trade treaty with Washington. He opposed conscription in 1917 and held Quebec for the Liberals while losing the rest. He died in Ottawa in February 1919 and fifty thousand people followed the coffin.
history.legacy: He governed Canada for fifteen years by persuasion, filled the West, and said the century would be Canada's.

personality.temperament: She outlived two husbands, both kings, and eight of her ten children. She went on crusade with the first, divorced him, married the second ten weeks later, rebelled against him with their sons and spent sixteen years in his custody. Freed at seventy, she rode across Europe to ransom one son and to fetch a bride for another. The troubadours sang in her court and the chroniclers, mostly clerics, disapproved of her in detail.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Angevin Empire, likes leaders with high loyalty and dislikes those whose cities waver; her own lands followed her from one crown to the other.

history.bio: Eleanor inherited Aquitaine, a third of France, at fifteen on her father's death in 1137 and was married within months to Louis VII of France. She went with him on the Second Crusade, quarrelled with him at Antioch, and had the marriage annulled in 1152 on grounds of kinship. Eight weeks later she married Henry Plantagenet, eleven years younger, who in 1154 became Henry II of England. Her dowry made him lord of more of France than the French king. She bore him eight children, including Richard the Lionheart and John, and in 1173 backed her sons' revolt against him; he kept her confined until his death in 1189. As queen mother she governed England during Richard's crusade, raised his ransom from the Emperor, and at eighty crossed the Pyrenees to bring her granddaughter Blanche to marry the heir of France. She died at Fontevraud in 1204 and lies there in effigy, reading a book.
history.legacy: She carried a third of France from one crown to the other and outlasted every man who tried to rule her.

civInfo.historical_background: Eleanor of Aquitaine (c. 1122-1204) was one of medieval Europe's most powerful women, first as Queen of France through her marriage to Louis VII and later, after that marriage was annulled, as Queen of England through her marriage to Henry II — the basis for Civ VI's unusual choice to let players pick either civilization for her. She ruled vast territories in her own right as Duchess of Aquitaine, presided over a famously sophisticated court associated with the culture of courtly love (the namesake of her 'Court of Love' ability), and later backed her sons' rebellions against Henry II, spending years imprisoned as a result. Her personal patronage of troubadours, poets, and the arts across both French and English courts underlies her Great Works/Loyalty-pressure-based path to peacefully absorbing rival cities.

conditionCost: Tundra dependency
note: Great Writers and Artists are permanent assets. Turns dead terrain into a Great Person engine.

dates.display: r. 1682 to 1725 (sole rule from 1696; Emperor from 1721)

history.polity: Tsardom of Russia; Russian Empire from 1721

personality.temperament: He stood over two metres tall, worked as a ship's carpenter in Holland under a false name, pulled teeth as a hobby, drank with a mock synod of drunkards, and shaved the beards off his nobles with his own hand. He built a capital on a swamp and ordered his subjects into it. He had his son tortured to death for treason. He learned everything he could from the West and used it against everyone who stood in his way, which included most of Russia.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Westernizer, likes leaders who lead him in science and culture and dislikes those behind him; he went to Europe to learn and came back to force it.

history.bio: Peter Alexeyevich was born in 1672 and proclaimed tsar at ten, jointly with his half-brother Ivan and under the regency of his half-sister Sophia, whom he overthrew in 1689. He took Azov from the Turks in 1696 and in 1697 travelled through Europe incognito, working in the Dutch and English shipyards and recruiting engineers. He came home to crush the streltsy revolt with mass executions and to force Western dress, the Julian calendar and a beard tax on the boyars. In 1700 he went to war with Sweden; after the defeat at Narva he rebuilt the army on European lines, founded St Petersburg on the Neva marsh in 1703, and at Poltava in 1709 destroyed Charles XII's army. The peace of Nystad in 1721 gave Russia the Baltic coast and Peter the title of emperor. He built the navy, the Senate, the Table of Ranks, the Academy of Sciences and the first Russian newspaper. His son Alexei died under interrogation in 1718. Peter died in February 1725, at fifty-two, without naming an heir.
history.legacy: He dragged Russia into Europe by the beard and built its capital on a marsh with the bones of the men who dug it.

civInfo.historical_background: Peter I ('Peter the Great', 1672-1725) ruled Russia (first as Tsar, later as Emperor) and pursued an aggressive campaign to modernize and Westernize the country, including a famous 1697-98 'Grand Embassy' tour of Western Europe — traveling incognito to study shipbuilding, military technology, and administration — that directly inspires his in-game leader ability and 'Westernizer' agenda. He founded St. Petersburg as a new, Western-facing capital, built Russia's first modern navy, and reformed the army, bureaucracy, and calendar. His reign's expansionist, cold-climate character (fighting the Great Northern War partly in harsh winter conditions) is echoed by Russia's tundra-friendly, territory-grabbing civilization ability.

expansionOrigin: Khmer and Indonesia Civilization & Scenario Pack

personality.temperament: His face is the one carved two hundred times on the towers of the Bayon, eyes half closed, mouth in a slight smile, and probably his portrait. He came to power late, after the Cham had sacked Angkor, drove them out and built more in thirty-seven years than any Khmer king before him: a walled city, a temple for his mother, a temple for his father, a hundred hospitals, rest houses along every road. An inscription says he suffered from the illnesses of his subjects more than from his own.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Monsoon Season, likes leaders with large city populations and dislikes those with small ones; his reign fed Angkor's million from its reservoirs.

history.bio: Jayavarman was a prince of the Khmer royal house who spent his middle years in Champa, the kingdom on the coast of what is now Vietnam, and was nearly sixty when a Cham fleet sailed up the Tonlé Sap and sacked Angkor in 1177. He returned, raised an army, defeated the Cham on the lake and in the field, and was crowned in 1181. He then invaded Champa itself and ruled it for twenty years. At home he built Angkor Thom, a walled capital with the Bayon at its centre, and the temple monasteries of Ta Prohm and Preah Khan, dedicated to his mother and father; he built one hundred and two hospitals and one hundred and twenty-one rest houses, and roads with stone bridges to link them. He made Mahayana Buddhism the state religion in a Hindu kingdom. The building emptied the treasury and the labour of a generation, and his successors reversed his faith and defaced his images. He died around 1218, in his nineties.
history.legacy: He rebuilt Angkor from a sack and left more stone, more hospitals and more roads than any king of Cambodia.

His combination of massive water-management infrastructure and prolific religious construction is directly reflected in the Khmer's in-game focus on Holy Sites, Aqueducts, and river-based city growth.
