history.polity: Ayyubid Sultanate (Egypt, Syria, Upper Mesopotamia, Hejaz, Yemen)

personality.temperament: A Kurdish soldier's son who did not want Egypt and was sent there by his uncle, he found himself vizier of a Shia caliphate and quietly ended it. He gave away so much that his treasury held one gold piece when he died. He took Jerusalem without a massacre, ransomed the poor, and let the Christians leave with their goods; the crusaders had killed everyone in it eighty-eight years before. He sent Richard the Lionheart fruit and snow when he was ill and two horses when his was killed. He had the Templars and Hospitallers beheaded after Hattin.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Ayyubid Dynasty, likes leaders who follow his religion and dislikes those who hold cities of another faith near him; he spent his life gathering Islam's lands against the crusaders.

history.bio: Yusuf ibn Ayyub was born at Tikrit in 1137 or 1138 and rose in the service of Nur ad-Din of Damascus. Sent to Egypt with his uncle Shirkuh in 1164, he succeeded him as vizier to the Fatimid caliph in 1169 and in 1171 abolished the Fatimid caliphate, restoring Egypt to Sunni allegiance. On Nur ad-Din's death in 1174 he took Damascus, then Aleppo in 1183 and Mosul in 1186, uniting the Muslim lands around the crusader kingdom for the first time. On 4 July 1187 at the Horns of Hattin he destroyed the army of Jerusalem, and on 2 October the city surrendered on terms. The Third Crusade followed; Richard of England retook Acre and beat him at Arsuf, but could not take Jerusalem, and the treaty of 1192 left it in Saladin's hands with the coast to the Franks. He died in Damascus on 4 March 1193 and was buried beside the Umayyad mosque. Dante put him in Limbo among the virtuous pagans, the only Muslim ruler Europe chose to admire.
history.legacy: He united Egypt and Syria, retook Jerusalem without a massacre, and died with one gold coin in the treasury.

civInfo.historical_background: Saladin (Salah ad-Din, c. 1137-1193) was the Kurdish founder of the Ayyubid dynasty who unified Egypt and Syria under his rule and became the preeminent Muslim leader of the Crusades. He is best remembered for recapturing Jerusalem from the Crusader states in 1187 and for his chivalrous conduct toward defeated enemies, including Richard the Lionheart, which earned him a reputation for both military skill and honor across cultures. His deep association with founding and defending a shared faith across a wide territory underlies Arabia's in-game identity as the civilization most reliably able to found and spread a religion.

name: Gandhi
conditionCost: Must stay at peace; scales with other civs founding religions

dates.display: led the Indian independence movement 1915 to 1947

history.polity: British India; the Indian independence movement
titles: Leader of the Indian National Congress

personality.temperament: He called his autobiography the story of his experiments with truth, and he ran the experiments on himself: diet, celibacy, silence, fasting to the edge of death to stop a riot. He was a lawyer who dressed as a peasant, a Hindu who read the Sermon on the Mount, and a man who answered an empire's police with a march to the sea to make salt. He was shot by a Hindu who thought him too soft on Muslims.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Peacekeeper, likes leaders at peace and refuses to forgive warmongers; the historical Gandhi built a national movement on non-violence.

history.bio: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born in Porbandar in 1869, trained as a barrister in London, and spent twenty-one years in South Africa, where he was thrown off a train for his colour and began the campaigns of civil disobedience he named satyagraha. He returned to India in 1915. He led the non-cooperation movement of 1920, the Salt March of 1930, walking 240 miles to the sea to break the British monopoly, and the Quit India campaign of 1942, and he spent more than six years of his life in prison for them. He worked for the untouchables, for village industry and for Hindu-Muslim unity, and he fasted against the violence of partition in 1947 while the country he had freed divided itself in blood. On 30 January 1948 Nathuram Godse shot him three times at a prayer meeting in Delhi. He held no office and commanded no army. Independent India has his face on every banknote.
history.legacy: He freed a nation without an army and was killed by one of his own for the peace he kept.

quote.text: The weak can never forgive. Forgiveness is the attribute of the strong.

civInfo.historical_background: Mohandas 'Mahatma' Gandhi (1869-1948) led India's independence movement from British colonial rule through a philosophy of nonviolent civil disobedience, or satyagraha ('truth-force'), that inspired later civil rights movements worldwide. A devout advocate of religious pluralism and tolerance between India's Hindu and Muslim communities, he was assassinated in 1948 shortly after independence was achieved. His commitment to nonviolence and interfaith coexistence is directly named in his leader ability (Satyagraha) and echoed in India's civilization ability, which rewards embracing many religions rather than enforcing one.

titles: Conquering Lion of the Tribe of Judah

personality.temperament: He spent ten years as a hostage of the emperor who had killed his father, escaped, and waited twenty more to take the crown. He bought rifles from every European power that would sell them and let each one think he was its client. When Italy claimed a treaty made Ethiopia its protectorate he denounced the Italian text, marched north with a hundred thousand men, and at Adwa destroyed the only European army ever beaten decisively by an African one in the age of empire. He then built a railway, a bank, a school and a telephone.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Mountain Lion, likes leaders who settle on hills and dislikes those who settle in his highlands; Ethiopia's independence was its mountains.

history.bio: Sahle Maryam was born in 1844, heir to the kingdom of Shewa, and was held at the court of Emperor Tewodros II from 1855 to 1865, when he escaped and took his father's throne. He expanded Shewa south and east, founded Addis Ababa in 1886, and was crowned emperor of Ethiopia in 1889 as Menelik II on the death of Yohannes IV. That year he signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy; the Italian text made Ethiopia a protectorate, the Amharic did not, and when Rome insisted he repudiated it in 1893. At Adwa on 1 March 1896 his army of about a hundred thousand destroyed an Italian force of seventeen thousand, and Italy recognised Ethiopia's full independence by the treaty of October. He then doubled the empire's territory by conquest in the south, conquests that his subjects there remember as such, and brought in the Djibouti railway, the first bank, the first modern school, electricity and the telephone. A stroke left him incapable from 1909; he died in December 1913.
history.legacy: He beat a European army at Adwa and kept Ethiopia the one African state that was never a colony.

civInfo.historical_background: Menelik II (reigned 1889-1913) was Emperor of Ethiopia who modernized the country's military and infrastructure while decisively defeating an invading Italian army at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, preserving Ethiopian sovereignty during the era of European colonization of Africa. His reign built on centuries of Ethiopian Christian tradition, including the rock-hewn churches carved into hillsides at places like Lalibela centuries earlier, and expanded the empire's territory significantly. The in-game emphasis on Hills, Faith, and rock-hewn architecture directly reflects Ethiopia's highland geography and its long Christian religious heritage.

expansionOrigin: Khmer and Indonesia Civilization & Scenario Pack
conditionCost: Water-heavy map required; dead on continents

personality.temperament: The Javanese chronicles call her Tribhuwana, ruler of the three worlds, and Gitarja is the childhood name the Pararaton preserves. She took the throne when her brother died without a son, put down a rebellion in person, and appointed as chief minister Gajah Mada, who swore an oath not to taste spice until the archipelago was hers. She let him keep it. She is shown in temple statuary as the goddess Parvati.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Exalted Goddess of the Three Worlds, likes leaders who hold faith and dislikes those with none; Majapahit's queen was carved as a goddess in her own lifetime.

history.bio: Dyah Gitarja was the daughter of Raden Wijaya, founder of Majapahit, and of Gayatri Rajapatni, a princess of the older kingdom of Singhasari. When her half-brother Jayanegara was murdered in 1328 the succession passed through her mother, who had become a Buddhist nun, and Gitarja ruled in her name under the title Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi. In 1331 she led the army herself against the rebellion of Sadeng and Keta in eastern Java. She raised Gajah Mada to mahapatih, chief minister, in 1334, and under his Palapa oath Majapahit took Bali in 1343 and sent fleets to Sumatra, Borneo and the Malay coast. She abdicated in 1350 when her mother died and the regency ended, and her son Hayam Wuruk reigned over the empire at its height. She lived on at court for two decades more. Her memorial statue at Candi Rimbi shows her as Parvati with four arms.
history.legacy: She took Majapahit from a murdered brother and handed her son the largest sea empire in Southeast Asian history.

civInfo.historical_background: Gitarja (Dyah Gitarja, also known as Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi, reigned 1328-1350) was a queen of the Majapahit Empire, one of the last and largest Hindu-Buddhist thalassocratic empires of maritime Southeast Asia, centered on Java. Under her rule and that of her son Hayam Wuruk, Majapahit extended influence across a vast archipelago through naval power and control of inter-island trade routes rather than contiguous land conquest. This archipelago-spanning, sea-based model of statecraft is the basis for Indonesia's in-game focus on coastal adjacency bonuses, naval units, and an agenda that rewards leaving small islands to Indonesia's control.

name: Jadwiga
conditionCost: Guaranteed diplomatic hostility from every neighbor

personality.temperament: She was crowned king, not queen, at ten, so that no husband could claim the crown over her. At twelve she gave up the Habsburg prince she had been promised and married the pagan grand duke of Lithuania, who was baptised for the purpose, and the chronicles treat the marriage as a sacrifice she made for the conversion of a nation. She spoke six languages, founded a theology faculty at Kraków, and sold her jewels to refound the university. She died at twenty-five, days after her only child.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Saint, likes leaders who follow her religion and dislikes those who spread another; her marriage converted Lithuania, the last pagan state in Europe.

history.bio: Jadwiga was the younger daughter of Louis I of Hungary and Poland, of the Angevin house, and was crowned at Kraków in October 1384 at the age of ten with the title of king, since Polish law knew no reigning queen. The Polish lords broke her childhood betrothal to William of Habsburg and in 1386 married her to Jogaila, grand duke of Lithuania, who accepted baptism as Władysław and was crowned beside her. The union of the two crowns created the largest state in Europe and lasted, in one form or another, until 1795. She ruled in her own right, negotiating with the Teutonic Knights, reconciling Jogaila with his cousin Vytautas, and leading an army into Ruthenia in 1387. She was a patron of scholars and translators and endowed the University of Kraków from her estate. She died on 17 July 1399, weeks after giving birth to a daughter who did not live. Poland venerated her at once; the Church canonised her in 1997.
history.legacy: She was crowned king at ten, married for a nation's conversion at twelve, and died at twenty-five a saint.

A devoted patron of the Church, she funded the restoration of Kraków's university and pushed for the Christianization of pagan Lithuania. Her role in forging a lasting personal union between two realms is echoed in the leader ability's name, Lithuanian Union, while her religious patronage is reflected in her Faith-focused agenda and Relic bonuses.

planSummary.one_line: Found a religion, walk a Missionary into the nearest rival's border city, and the moment it converts, ride Horsemen and Knights through its Walls as if they were not there. Every kill spreads the religion to the next city, so the war converts its own next target.

name: Basil II
expansionOrigin: New Frontier Pass: Byzantium & Gaul Pack
conditionCost: Requires founding a religion AND spreading it to the target first
note: Two-step prerequisite before the combat bonus exists. Slow to come online, brutal once it does.

personality.temperament: Psellos, who knew men who had served him, described an emperor who gave up wine, women, jewels and conversation, slept on the ground with his soldiers, and spoke in short sentences in a soldier's voice. He trusted no aristocrat after two of them tried to take his throne, and he ruled through eunuchs and the army. He laughed rarely. He campaigned every year of his adult life.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Porphyrogénnētos, respects leaders with strong cavalry and distrusts those who neglect it; Basil's empire was built on the armoured horse.

history.bio: Basil was born in the purple chamber of the palace in 958 and crowned co-emperor at two. He did not rule until 976, and for the first thirteen years of his reign the generals Skleros and Phokas each rose against him; he broke the second at Abydos in 989 with six thousand Varangians sent by Vladimir of Kiev, to whom he gave his sister in marriage and the Orthodox faith. He then turned on Bulgaria and fought it for thirty years. At Kleidion in 1014 he took fourteen thousand prisoners and, by the chroniclers' account, blinded ninety-nine of every hundred and sent them home led by the hundredth; Tsar Samuel died at the sight. Bulgaria fell in 1018 and the Danube was Rome's frontier again. He annexed Armenian lands, held Syria against the Fatimids, and filled a treasury that his heirs emptied in a generation. He never married and died in 1025 planning an expedition to Sicily.
history.legacy: He ruled for forty-nine years, restored the Danube frontier, and left an empire at its height to heirs who could not hold it.

civInfo.historical_background: Basil II (reigned 976-1025) was one of the Byzantine Empire's most formidable emperors, expanding its borders to their greatest extent since Justinian through decades of relentless campaigning, most famously his prolonged conquest of the First Bulgarian Empire, which earned him the epithet 'Bulgar-Slayer.' Born 'porphyrogennetos' ('born in the purple'), meaning born to a reigning emperor in the palace's porphyry chamber, he ruled as a soldier-emperor who tied military success closely to Orthodox Christian identity and left the treasury and empire stronger than he found them. His fusion of religious authority with battlefield conquest is captured directly in his leader ability's name and its focus on converting military victories into religious dominance.

planSummary.one_line: Found a religion early, beeline Gunpowder, and walk Conquistadors with Missionaries on their tiles into the nearest civilization that worships something else. Every city they take converts on capture, and every civilization that already follows you is left alone, because it already counts toward the win.

name: Philip II
conditionCost: Bonus only applies against differently-faithed civs
note: If a neighbor converts to your religion, your combat bonus against them evaporates.

history.polity: Spanish Empire (Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Naples, Sicily, Milan, the Americas, the Philippines)

personality.temperament: He governed the first empire on which the sun never set from a desk, reading and annotating every dispatch himself, in a monastery-palace he built in the hills above Madrid with his bedroom opening onto the high altar. He married four times, lost Elizabeth of England to heresy and the Netherlands to revolt, bankrupted the treasury four times, and sent an Armada that the wind destroyed. He wore black and distrusted everyone, including, with reason, his secretaries.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Counter Reformer, likes leaders who follow his religion and will not tolerate those who spread another into his cities; the Spanish Inquisition was his instrument.

history.bio: Philip was born at Valladolid in 1527, the son of the Emperor Charles V, and was raised to rule from childhood. His father gave him Naples and Milan, then the Netherlands, then in 1556 Spain and the Indies. He had married Mary I of England in 1554 and was king consort there until her death in 1558. He won at Saint-Quentin, built El Escorial from 1563 as palace, monastery and tomb, and from 1568 fought the revolt of the Netherlands that his taxation and his heresy laws had provoked; the Duke of Alba's Council of Blood executed over a thousand. His fleet beat the Turks at Lepanto in 1571. In 1580 he took the Portuguese crown by inheritance and arms. In 1588 he sent the Armada against Elizabeth and lost a third of it. He defaulted on his debts in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596, the silver of Potosí notwithstanding. He died at El Escorial in September 1598 after fifty-three days of illness, having governed for forty-two years with a pen.
history.legacy: He ruled the first global empire from a desk in a monastery and bankrupted it four times in the service of his faith.

civInfo.historical_background: Philip II of Spain (reigned 1556-1598) ruled the largest empire the world had yet seen, spanning territories in Europe, the Americas, Africa, and Asia, funded in large part by silver shipped home in fleets from the New World. A fiercely devout Catholic monarch, he positioned himself as Europe's foremost defender of the Counter-Reformation, waging war against Protestant England and the Dutch rebels and overseeing the Spanish Inquisition's campaign against heresy. His combination of a religiously enforced empire and treasure-fleet-driven wealth is reflected directly in Spain's civilization ability and Philip's religious-conformity agenda and Inquisitor bonus.

planSummary.one_line: Keep the Era Score above the Golden Age line every era, found a religion and carry it into the city-states, and let every envoy count twice until Georgia is suzerain of half the map. The Faith and the suzerainties then win the World Congress; if the chain breaks, the same religion still wins on its own.

name: Tamar
leaderTitle: King of Kings and Queen of Queens of Georgia
conditionCost: Envoy and wall investment; Golden Age chain breaks if an era is missed
note: Chained bonuses are fragile. One Normal Age resets the whole compounding sequence.

titles: King of Kings and Queen of Queens of Georgia

personality.temperament: The chronicle of her reign calls her mepe, king, and says the nobles who made her accept a council made her accept a husband too, a Russian prince who drank and rebelled and was sent away twice. Her second husband, an Alan prince raised at her court, won her wars. She is painted in the monasteries with a long face and a long crown, and the poet Rustaveli dedicated The Knight in the Panther's Skin to her. The Church made her a saint.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Glory of the World, likes leaders who send envoys to the city-states she protects and dislikes those who take them; Georgia's golden age was an age of protectorates.

history.bio: Tamar was crowned co-ruler by her father George III in 1178, against the opposition of the nobles, and succeeded him in 1184. The aristocracy forced her to dismiss her father's ministers, accept a council, and marry Yuri Bogolyubsky of Vladimir, whom she divorced for drunkenness in 1187 and whose two rebellions she defeated. She married David Soslan, an Alan prince, in 1189, and with him and the brothers Zakare and Ivane Mkhargrdzeli as generals won at Shamkor in 1195 and Basiani in 1203 over the Muslim rulers of Azerbaijan and Anatolia, took Kars, and in 1204 set her kinsman Alexios Komnenos on the throne of Trebizond as a client of Georgia. Her realm ran from the Black Sea to the Caspian and from the Caucasus to Erzurum. Churches, monasteries, the cave city of Vardzia and the epic of Rustaveli belong to her reign. She died in January 1213; her burial place was hidden and has not been found.
history.legacy: She ruled Georgia at the height of its power as king in title and queen in fact, and the Church made her a saint.

civInfo.name: Tamar

leader_ability.text: Tamar gains Faith from combat victories based on the strength of the defeated unit, and after adopting Theology she can declare a special Protectorate War that doubles Faith output for a period and makes envoys sent to city-states that share Georgia's majority religion count double, tying military success to religious and diplomatic gains.

agenda.name: Narikala Fortress
agenda.text: Tamar fortifies her cities with the strongest available Walls and dislikes civilizations that leave their cities poorly defended.

civ_ability.name: Strength in Unity
civ_ability.text: Georgia earns bonus Era Score for Dedications made at the start of Golden and Heroic Ages and gains extra Production toward building Walls, helping it weather the Loyalty and warfare pressures of the Rise and Fall systems.

unique_units.name: Khevsur
unique_units.notes: A Medieval-era unit with a large Combat Strength bonus on Hills and no hill movement penalty, giving Georgia a strong defensive infantry option in its mountainous heartland.

unique_infrastructure.name: Tsikhe

civInfo.historical_background: Tamar the Great (reigned 1184-1213) presided over the political, military, and cultural high point of the medieval Kingdom of Georgia, expanding its borders through successful campaigns while overseeing a flourishing of Georgian art, architecture, and literature, including the national epic 'The Knight in the Panther's Skin.' She ruled from heavily fortified strongholds carved into the Caucasus mountains, such as the Narikala fortress overlooking Tbilisi, defending her kingdom against Seljuk and other regional powers. Her reign's reputation for both formidable defenses and religious devotion (Georgia being one of the world's oldest Christian states) is reflected in her fortress-building agenda and Faith-generating combat ability.

structure.goal: This replaces the turn list entirely. The guide is this loop plus the era checkpoints.
per_turn_check: Read Own era score approaching Golden Age threshold, AND ally-under-attack status.
Green band: continue current build. No action.
Amber band: begin the correction now. Amber is the acting band; red is the failing band.
Red band: the ability is off or about to be. Everything else is deprioritized until it clears.
structure.opportunity_trigger: For reactive leaders (Lautaro, Tamar, John Curtin), add a second watched value: the external condition that switches the ability on. The guide must state what to do during the periods it is off, because those periods are most of the game.

structure.goal: Re-read the role. Monitor leaders change what the stat means across eras.
steps: Ancient/Classical: Walls and envoy investment. Slow start.
Medieval/Renaissance: Golden Age chaining at full effect.
Industrial/Modern: Strong while the chain holds, fragile if broken.
Atomic/Information: Dependent on an unbroken sequence.

abort_branch.trigger: Watched stat sits in the red band for more than roughly 15 turns with no recovery path.
actions: Stop paying the Envoy and wall investment; Golden Age chain breaks if an era is missed. If the bonus is unreachable, its price is pure loss.
Rebuild as a generic civ around whatever the monitored strategy already produced.

anti_patterns: Writing this shape as a turn-by-turn build order. It is the wrong instrument.
Stating the green band only. Players need the amber threshold, because that is where action is still cheap.

planSummary.one_line: Settle the desert, send every Trade Route abroad, buy every building with Gold and every Suguba building with Faith, and never put a unit or a building in the Production queue. The desert City Centers and Desert Folklore pay the Apostles; the Gold pays everything else, including the votes if the religion stalls.

name: Mansa Musa
conditionCost: Severe Production penalty and desert dependency
note: Buys permanence with gold instead of building it. Works, but only if the gold never stops.

titles: Lord of the Mines of Wangara

personality.temperament: He went to Mecca in 1324 with sixty thousand people and a hundred camels of gold, gave so much away in Cairo that the price of gold fell for a decade, and came back with architects and scholars. Arab writers who met him describe a man of dignity and few words who kept a hall of silent audience and would not be seen to eat. His empire ran on salt from the north and gold from the south and the law of the Quran at every stop between.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Gold and Salt, likes leaders who send him trade routes and dislikes those who do not; the whole of Mali was built on the caravans.

history.bio: Musa came to the throne of Mali in 1312 when his predecessor Abu Bakr II sailed into the Atlantic with a fleet and did not come back, or so Musa told the Egyptians. Mali already held the gold fields of Bambuk and Bure and the salt mines of Taghaza; Musa extended it to Gao and Timbuktu and governed it through provincial governors and a standing army. In 1324 he made the pilgrimage to Mecca by way of Cairo, where his spending in gold dust and gifts flooded the market and depressed the metal's value for years; the chronicler al-Umari recorded it a dozen years later from witnesses. He returned with the Andalusian architect al-Sahili and with Maliki jurists, built the Djinguereber mosque at Timbuktu and the great mosque at Gao, and made Timbuktu a centre of learning. The Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows him seated on a throne in the middle of Africa holding a nugget. He died around 1337. His wealth is beyond estimate, which is why it is called the greatest in history.
history.legacy: He took so much gold to Mecca that Cairo's markets did not recover for years, and he came back with scholars.

terrain.why: Sahel Merchants and the Suguba want desert; production is the price
Food beside the desert
Mines in the one place Mali can build them

affinity.barbarianStance: Mali cannot build a cheap army; it buys one. Walls bought with gold in every city, Mandekalu Cavalry to escort traders, and camps left alone unless a trader route crosses them.

civInfo.name: Mansa Musa

leader_ability.name: Sahel Merchants
leader_ability.text: International Trade Routes gain bonus Gold for every flat Desert tile in their origin city, and entering a Golden or Heroic Age grants Mali a permanent extra Trade Route slot, rewarding a gold-focused desert trading empire.

agenda.name: Lord of the Mines
agenda.text: Mansa Musa single-mindedly pursues Gold accumulation and looks unfavorably on civilizations with weak Gold income.

civ_ability.name: Songs of the Jeli
civ_ability.text: Mali's City Centers gain extra Faith and Food for adjacent Desert and Desert Hills tiles, Commercial Hub buildings can be purchased with Faith, and Mines produce more Gold at the cost of reduced Production, in exchange for a Production penalty on units and buildings overall.

unique_units.name: Mandekalu Cavalry
unique_units.notes: A cavalry unit well-suited to protecting Mali's lucrative trade routes across the desert.

unique_infrastructure.name: Suguba
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Commercial Hub and provides discounts on Gold and Faith purchases made in its city, reinforcing Mali's wealth-and-Faith hybrid economy.

civInfo.historical_background: Mansa Musa I (reigned c. 1312-1337) ruled the West African Mali Empire at the height of its wealth and power, controlling lucrative trans-Saharan trade routes in gold and salt. His 1324-1325 pilgrimage to Mecca became legendary for its extravagance—he reportedly distributed so much gold along the way that he temporarily depressed its value in the regions he passed through—cementing his reputation as perhaps the wealthiest individual in history. He also invested heavily in Islamic scholarship and architecture, transforming Timbuktu into a major center of learning. His singular association with fabulous gold wealth built on desert trade routes is the direct inspiration for his Gold-obsessed agenda and Mali's desert-and-trade-focused civilization ability.

planSummary.one_line: Grow four river cities on Granaries, Aqueducts and Farms before running a single project, then push them over Population 10 one at a time with the Lijia Food project and turn each crossing into a University and a Researcher. Nothing happens for eighty turns, and then the Science chart turns.

name: Yongle
expansionOrigin: Leader Pass: Rulers of China Pack
conditionCost: Project turns spent reaching pop thresholds are turns not spent building
note: Threshold-gated rather than gradual. Nothing happens, then everything does.

history.faith: Chinese state religion; patron of Buddhism and Taoism

personality.temperament: He took the throne from his nephew in a three-year civil war and had the scholar who refused to write the accession edict executed with his family to the tenth degree, nine hundred people. He then moved the capital to Beijing and built the Forbidden City, sent Zheng He's treasure fleets to Africa, commissioned an encyclopaedia of eleven thousand volumes, invaded Vietnam and led five campaigns into Mongolia in person. He died on the last one. The Ming kept his capital and burned his fleet.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Treasure Fleet, likes leaders whose trade routes bring him gold and dislikes those who send none; the fleets sailed to collect tribute.

history.bio: Zhu Di was the fourth son of the Hongwu Emperor, founder of the Ming, and was made Prince of Yan at Beijing to hold the northern frontier against the Mongols. When his father died in 1398 the throne passed to a grandson, the Jianwen Emperor, who began to strip the princes of their power. Zhu Di rebelled in 1399 and in 1402 took Nanjing; his nephew vanished in the palace fire. He took the reign name Yongle, perpetual happiness, and purged the court. From 1406 he built the Forbidden City and in 1421 moved the capital to Beijing, reopened the Grand Canal to feed it, and raised the Porcelain Tower at Nanjing. He sent the eunuch admiral Zheng He on six voyages with fleets of three hundred ships to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa. He annexed Vietnam in 1407, commissioned the Yongle Encyclopaedia, and led five expeditions into the steppe, dying on the return from the last in August 1424. His grandson ended the voyages.
history.legacy: He seized the throne, built Beijing, and sent the largest fleet the world had seen to Africa; his heirs kept the city and sank the fleet.

terrain.why: Production and the Great Wall
Growth for the Lijia's yields-to-gold conversion

affinity.barbarianStance: Yongle's cities convert yields to gold and buy what they need. Buy walls in the border cities, clear the camp that sees the capital, and use Crouching Tigers behind the wall.

civInfo.name: Yongle

leader_ability.name: Lijia
leader_ability.text: Yongle's cities gain access to unique Lijia projects that convert a share of Production into Food, Faith, or Gold, and cities with high Population generate extra Gold, Science, and Culture per Citizen, rewarding large, well-developed Chinese cities.

agenda.name: Yinding
agenda.text: Yongle favors civilizations running a positive Gold income and dislikes those running a Gold deficit.

civ_ability.name: Dynastic Cycle
civ_ability.text: China's Eurekas and Inspirations provide a larger boost toward the cost of the technology or civic they unlock, and completing a Wonder grants a free Eureka and Inspiration, accelerating China's overall tech and civic progress.

unique_units.name: Crouching Tiger Cannon
unique_units.notes: An early gunpowder siege unit that does not require the Niter resource normally needed by the Bombard, letting China field powerful siege weapons without a strategic resource dependency.

unique_infrastructure.name: Great Wall
unique_infrastructure.notes: A unique tile improvement built on Hills that provides early defense and Gold, later converting to Culture and Tourism, and gains bonuses for connecting to adjacent Great Wall segments.

civInfo.historical_background: The Yongle Emperor (reigned 1402-1424) was the third emperor of China's Ming dynasty, who seized the throne from his nephew and went on to relocate the capital to Beijing, where he commissioned the Forbidden City. He commissioned the enormous 'Yongle Encyclopedia' compiling China's accumulated knowledge, expanded and fortified sections of the Great Wall, and sponsored Admiral Zheng He's famous treasure-fleet voyages that projected Chinese naval power and trade across the Indian Ocean. Yongle is presented in Civilization VI as an alternate persona for China alongside the base game's Qin Shi Huang, added later via the Leader Pass DLC program, with his in-game focus on Production-conversion projects and large, wealthy cities reflecting his ambitious capital-building and encyclopedic era.

structure.goal: A single decision point, not a phase.
tests: Gate open AND staging complete: proceed to Post-Gate.
Gate open, staging incomplete: do not proceed. Finish staging. An unstaged opening wastes the gate entirely.

abort_branch.trigger: Gate opens with staging incomplete and a rival is already at parity.

template.fail_state: The gate opened, the window closed, and the strategy never ran. The pre-gate phase was treated as filler and produced nothing usable.

Omitting the closing window. Gate leaders have two deadlines, not one.

planSummary.one_line: Settle every coast on the home continent as fast as the Cothon can pump Settlers, because none of those cities can ever flip, then take the pump overseas and move the capital only when the second continent holds more of your cities than the first. Twelve Harbors and twelve Campuses win the Science race by weight.

name: Dido
conditionCost: Coastal settling; capital relocation has a real opportunity cost
note: Loyalty immunity removes the single biggest constraint on overseas expansion.

dates.display: fl. c. 814 BCE (traditional founding of Carthage)
dates.historicity: legendary; Carthage's founding is historical, its founder is tradition

history.polity: Carthage, a Phoenician colony of Tyre

personality.temperament: The tradition remembers a woman who outwitted a brother, a landlord and a god. She fled Tyre with her husband's treasure and a company of nobles, asked the Libyan king for as much land as an ox-hide would cover, and cut the hide into a thread that enclosed a hill. Virgil gave her a Trojan lover and a funeral pyre; the Carthaginian version, lost with the city, made her die rather than marry a Libyan king.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Sicilian Wars, likes leaders who settle away from her and dislikes those who settle near her coast; the historical Carthage fought Greece for Sicily for three centuries.

history.bio: Elissa, called Dido, was by tradition a princess of Tyre, sister of King Pygmalion, who murdered her husband the priest Acerbas for his gold. She took the gold and a company of followers, sailed west by way of Cyprus, and landed on the coast of Libya near the modern city of Tunis. There she bought from the Berber king Iarbas the land an ox-hide could cover and, cutting it into strips, enclosed the hill called Byrsa, the hide. The city founded there, Qart-hadasht, the new city, grew into Carthage, the greatest trading power of the western Mediterranean, with harbours, a navy, and colonies from Spain to Sicily. The founding date given by ancient writers is 814 BCE, and archaeology finds Phoenician settlement on the site by the late ninth century. Dido herself has left no inscription, no coin and no tomb. Timaeus told her story first; Virgil gave her to Aeneas; Carthage, which kept its own account, was burned by Rome in 146 BCE.
history.legacy: She founded the city that fought Rome for the Mediterranean, and Rome's poet gave her the only story of her that survives.

terrain.why: The Cothon and coastal cities on the home continent keep full loyalty
Growth for the coastal settler pump

cityStates.why: Venice, Hunza and Mogadishu multiply the Cothon's routes

affinity.barbarianStance: Coastal camps spawn galleys that pillage fishing boats. One Bireme on patrol handles them; inland camps are ignored unless a scout has seen your city.

civInfo.name: Dido

leader_ability.name: Founder of Carthage
leader_ability.text: Cities with a Cothon can use a unique project to relocate Phoenicia's capital there, and Dido gains extra Trade Route capacity and a Production bonus toward Districts in the city containing her Government Plaza, supporting a highly mobile, expansion-driven playstyle.

agenda.name: Sicilian Wars
agenda.text: Dido pursues coastal expansion for herself but dislikes rival civilizations that accumulate many coastal cities, echoing Carthage's historical rivalry with Greek colonies over Mediterranean coastlines.

civ_ability.name: Mediterranean Colonies
civ_ability.text: Coastal Phoenician cities founded on the same continent as the capital always have maximum Loyalty, embarked Settlers move faster and see farther with reduced embarkation costs, and Phoenicia starts with the Eureka for Writing already unlocked, making it exceptionally strong at rapid coastal settlement.

unique_units.name: Bireme
unique_units.notes: A faster, stronger naval melee unit that also shields nearby Traders from plundering, protecting Phoenicia's seaborne trade network.

unique_infrastructure.name: Cothon
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Harbor, boosts Production toward Settlers and naval units, heals naval units faster, and is required to relocate the Phoenician capital via Dido's leader ability.

civInfo.historical_background: Dido is the legendary founder and first queen of Carthage, said in classical tradition (notably Virgil's Aeneid) to have fled Phoenician Tyre and founded her new city on the North African coast around the 9th century BC, growing it into one of the ancient Mediterranean's great maritime trading powers. Carthage's power rested on an extensive network of coastal colonies and trade routes stretching across the Mediterranean, a legacy that eventually put it in prolonged conflict with Greek city-states in Sicily and, later, with Rome in the Punic Wars. Her legendary founding of a new city by the sea and Phoenicia's historical mastery of coastal colonization directly shape both her capital-relocating leader ability and the civilization's emphasis on rapid, loyal coastal settlement.

planSummary.one_line: Settle eight to ten cities in a tight coastal cluster, give each a Commercial Hub or Harbor so it adds a Trader, send the routes into a capital stacked with every district type, never trade abroad, and decide by turn 70 what the Culture, Science and Gold are for.

name: Tokugawa
conditionCost: International trade heavily penalized; forfeits foreign trade income entirely
note: Trades a whole mechanic away for a stronger version of a different one.

history.faith: Jōdo Buddhism; deified as a Shinto kami after death

personality.temperament: He spent his childhood as a hostage, his youth as a vassal of Nobunaga and his middle age as a vassal of Hideyoshi, and he waited. The Japanese proverb has Nobunaga pound the rice, Hideyoshi knead the dough, and Ieyasu eat the cake. He won the one battle that mattered, took the title of shogun, retired in two years so that his son's succession would be unquestioned, and then destroyed the last Toyotomi heir at Osaka. He wrote that life is like walking a long road with a heavy load, and that patience is the root of all quiet.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Sakoku, likes leaders who keep their trade and settlers away from his lands and dislikes those who send them near; his heirs closed Japan for two centuries.

history.bio: Matsudaira Takechiyo was born at Okazaki in 1543 and spent twelve years as a hostage of the Imagawa and Oda clans. He allied with Oda Nobunaga in 1561, took the name Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1567, survived his one great defeat at Mikatagahara in 1573, and after Nobunaga's death in 1582 submitted to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who moved him to the Kanto plain in 1590, where he built Edo. On Hideyoshi's death in 1598 he was the most powerful of the regents for the child heir, and on 21 October 1600 at Sekigahara he destroyed the western coalition in a single day. The emperor named him shogun in 1603. He abdicated in 1605 for his son Hidetada and governed from Sunpu, regulated the daimyo and the court, took control of foreign trade, began the suppression of Christianity, and in 1614 and 1615 besieged and burned Osaka Castle, ending the Toyotomi. He died in June 1616 and was enshrined at Nikkō as a god. His house ruled Japan until 1868.
history.legacy: He waited forty years for one battle, won it in a day, and founded a peace that lasted two hundred and fifty years.

terrain.why: Districts on coast; domestic trade routes pay more
Production for the Electronics Factory

cityStates.why: Muscat for amenities with Commercial Hubs

affinity.barbarianStance: Tokugawa's bonuses are domestic; a raid breaks the trade routes that pay him. Walls and Samurai on the coast, and every camp within five tiles cleared.

civInfo.name: Tokugawa

leader_ability.name: Bakuhan
leader_ability.text: Tokugawa's international Trade Routes suffer a penalty to all yields and Tourism, but his domestic Trade Routes grant bonus Culture, Science, and Gold for every specialty District at the destination, pushing Japan toward an inward-facing, isolationist economy built on strong domestic trade networks.

agenda.name: Sakoku
agenda.text: Tokugawa wants to remain safe from conquest, favoring civilizations that likewise avoid war and expansion by conquest, and he dislikes leaders who have captured other civilizations' capitals.

civ_ability.name: Meiji Restoration
civ_ability.text: Japanese Districts receive standard rather than reduced adjacency bonuses even when adjacency conditions would normally give a lesser bonus (such as on Hills or next to other districts), letting Japan cluster districts tightly for strong yields; cities near the capital also gain Amenities, with Tourism from Districts unlocked later after researching Flight.

unique_units.name: Samurai
unique_units.notes: A resilient melee unit that does not lose combat strength as it takes damage, letting it keep fighting effectively even when badly wounded.

unique_infrastructure.name: Electronics Factory
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Factory and extends bonus Production and Culture to nearby cities rather than only its own city, strengthening Japan's tightly clustered industrial cities.

civInfo.historical_background: Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543-1616) was the daimyo who emerged victorious from Japan's chaotic Sengoku ('Warring States') period after his decisive victory at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, founding the Tokugawa shogunate that would rule Japan for over 250 years. His government pursued a policy of strict social order and, under his successors, near-total national seclusion (sakoku), closing Japan off from most foreign trade and contact to preserve internal stability. Added to Civilization VI as an alternate persona for Japan alongside the base game's Hojo Tokimune, his in-game penalty to foreign trade paired with strong domestic trade bonuses, along with an agenda built around avoiding conquest, directly mirrors the historical isolationist Sakoku policy associated with his dynasty.

planSummary.one_line: Meet everyone, fill every Trade Route slot with a coastal foreign city, plant Feitorias in the hosts most likely to survive the game, and turn the Gold into Navigation Schools, Campuses and Research Labs. Audit the host cities every five turns, because the economy lives in other people's ports.

name: Joao III
leaderTitle: King of Portugal and the Algarves
conditionCost: Water map plus coastal foreign cities that must actually exist and stay reachable
note: Routes depend on other civs' city placement. Yields drop if targets are lost or conquered.

history.polity: Kingdom of Portugal and its overseas empire
titles: King of Portugal and the Algarves
Lord of Guinea and of the Conquest, Navigation and Commerce of Ethiopia, Arabia, Persia and India

personality.temperament: The Pious King was not a sailor and never left Portugal. He inherited an empire of forts and factories from Lisbon to the Spice Islands and spent his reign deciding which to keep. He brought the Inquisition to Portugal, sent the Jesuits to Goa and Japan, settled Brazil with captaincies, and gave up Moroccan fortresses the crown could no longer pay for. He married his sister to Charles V and his children died before him, all nine.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Navigator's Legacy, likes leaders who settle coasts and dislikes those who keep away from the sea; Portugal's whole empire was a line of harbours.

history.bio: João III succeeded his father Manuel I in December 1521, at nineteen, as king of a country of a million people that held the sea route to India. He reorganised the Estado da Índia, took Diu and Bassein, and opened trade with China at Macau and with Japan at Tanegashima in 1543. He divided Brazil into hereditary captaincies in 1534 and, when most of them failed, sent a royal governor to found Salvador in 1549. He invited the Society of Jesus to Portugal in 1540 and sent Francis Xavier east; he obtained the Inquisition from Rome in 1536 and it burned its first heretics in Lisbon in 1540. He abandoned Safim, Azamor and Arzila in Morocco, judging them unaffordable, and he fell into debt to the bankers of Antwerp for the rest. He died in June 1557, outlived by none of his children; the crown passed to his grandson Sebastião, a child of three.
history.legacy: He turned an age of discovery into an empire of administration, from Brazil to Japan, and buried every heir he had.

terrain.why: Portugal trades only with coastal cities; the Navigation School and Feitoria want harbours
Nau and Carracks cross it first

affinity.barbarianStance: Portugal's wealth is at sea and so are its raiders. One Nau per coast clears the galleys; land camps are cleared only when a scout has seen a city.

civInfo.name: Joao III

leader_ability.name: Porta do Cerco
leader_ability.text: All of João's units gain extra Sight, meeting a new civilization grants an additional Trade Route capacity, and Portugal automatically has Open Borders with all city-states, supporting an exploration-and-trade-focused playstyle from the earliest turns.

agenda.name: Navigator's Legacy
agenda.text: João III loves exploring the map and favors other civilizations that prioritize exploration as well.

civ_ability.name: Casa da Índia
civ_ability.text: Portuguese international Trade Routes can only target coastal cities or cities with a Harbor, but those routes gain a large yield bonus, and Portuguese Traders have increased range over water and can embark as soon as Trade Routes are unlocked, rewarding an ocean-spanning trade network.

unique_units.name: Nau
unique_units.notes: A naval unit with a free promotion and lower maintenance than the Caravel, and it carries charges to build the unique Feitoria improvement, linking exploration directly to Portugal's trade economy.

unique_infrastructure.name: Feitoria
unique_infrastructure.notes: Built only by a Nau on a foreign coastal city's tile next to a resource; Trade Routes sent to that city grant Portugal bonus Gold and Production, a unique way to profit from other civilizations' territory.

unique_infrastructure.name: Navigation School
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the University and boosts Production toward naval units in its city, supporting Portugal's seafaring, exploration-heavy strategy.

civInfo.historical_background: João III (reigned 1521-1557) ruled Portugal during the height of its overseas empire, consolidating and expanding the trading-post network established by his predecessors across the Atlantic, coastal Africa, India, and Southeast Asia through institutions like the Casa da Índia, which regulated the lucrative spice and goods trade with Portuguese Asia. His reign saw continued Portuguese exploration and colonization, including the beginnings of Portuguese Brazil's development, even as the crown increasingly relied on trade-post profits rather than large-scale territorial conquest. This coastal, trading-post-based model of empire—profit from controlled maritime trade routes rather than land conquest—is the direct basis for Portugal's Casa da Índia civilization ability and its unique Feitoria trading-post improvement.
